A good night’s sleep often begins with the choices you make before your head reaches the pillow. When evenings feel rushed and mornings start at different times, restful sleep can become harder to find. A useful place to begin is a routine you can repeat comfortably: give yourself enough time to sleep, keep regular hours, and make the transition from activity to rest a little gentler.

Start by choosing a realistic wake-up time and keeping it fairly consistent, including on weekends. Then protect enough time in your evening to get the sleep you need. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends allowing at least seven to eight hours and going to bed when you feel sleepy. Think about what this means for your actual schedule: an early alarm needs a suitably early end to the evening. [American Academy of Sleep Medicine](https://sleepeducation.org/healthy-sleep/healthy-sleep-habits/)

Your daytime habits deserve attention, too. Spend some time outdoors when possible, get regular physical activity, and seek natural daylight. These habits support your body’s daily rhythm. You could take a walk during lunch or spend part of your morning outside. Choose something that fits naturally into your day so that repeating it feels manageable. [NIH healthy sleep guidance](https://health.nih.gov/health-topics-a-z/healthy-sleep)

Pay attention to the timing of caffeine. Its effects can last up to eight hours, so an afternoon coffee may still interfere with sleep that night. If you suspect a connection, try moving your last caffeinated drink earlier. Keep evening meals comfortable in size as well; a large, heavy dinner close to bedtime can make settling down more difficult. [NHLBI healthy sleep habits](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/sleep-deprivation/healthy-sleep-habits)

As bedtime approaches, give yourself a predictable period to unwind. Dim the lights, close your work messages, and put your phone somewhere that makes casual scrolling less tempting. Read a few pages, listen to quiet music, or take a warm bath. A short routine is enough to begin with. The aim is to choose activities that help you relax and that you will want to repeat tomorrow. [NIH healthy sleep guidance](https://health.nih.gov/health-topics-a-z/healthy-sleep)

Make your bedroom comfortable for sleeping. Keep it cool, quiet, and dark, adjusting those conditions to your needs. Curtains can help with outside light, while a quieter room may require a conversation about household noise. Start with the disturbance you notice most. Solving one obvious problem can be a practical first step without turning bedtime into a complicated project. [NHLBI healthy sleep habits](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/sleep-deprivation/healthy-sleep-habits)

If you remain awake for roughly twenty minutes, get up and do something quiet in dim light until you feel sleepy again. Avoid reaching for stimulating entertainment or work. This approach helps strengthen the connection between your bed and sleep. [American Academy of Sleep Medicine](https://sleepeducation.org/healthy-sleep/healthy-sleep-habits/)

Persistent sleep difficulties deserve more than another adjustment to your evening routine. If trouble sleeping continues or affects your daily life, speak with a healthcare professional. For long-term insomnia, cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, or CBT-I, is usually recommended as the first treatment. [NHLBI insomnia treatment](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/insomnia/treatment)

Tonight, choose a manageable starting point: set tomorrow’s wake-up time, decide when to put your phone away, and leave yourself a quiet stretch before bed. Build from there as you learn which habits fit your life.

<<The 2000 Presidential Election>>

The 2000 presidential election between Republican George W. Bush and Democrat Al Gore became one of the closest and most controversial contests in American history. Although Gore won the national popular vote, the presidency depended on Florida, where an exceptionally narrow margin triggered recounts and intense legal battles.

Florida's voting problems exposed weaknesses in election administration. Confusing ballot designs, outdated equipment, and disputes over voter intent complicated the counting process. Images of officials inspecting partially punched ballots became symbols of the controversy. Both campaigns argued that their preferred procedures would protect fairness, while public confidence increasingly reflected partisan loyalties.

On December 12, the Supreme Court's decision in Bush v. Gore halted the ongoing recount, effectively securing Bush's victory. Florida's certified result gave him a lead of just 537 votes. Gore conceded the following day, emphasizing national unity while acknowledging his disagreement with the Court's resolution of the dispute.

The election's legacy extended beyond its immediate outcome. It prompted reforms to voting technology and election procedures, renewed criticism of the Electoral College, and intensified political polarization. Ultimately, the contest demonstrated how administrative details, judicial decisions, and constitutional structures can shape democratic outcomes when an electorate is evenly divided.

“The History of the World, as Told by Dogs” is a proposed three-credit undergraduate seminar that explores human history through the animals that have followed, guarded, fed beside, and occasionally bitten us. Open to students from all majors, the course asks: How does world history change when dogs move from the margins of the story to its center?

Across fourteen weeks, students will examine domestication, migration, agriculture, empire, industrialization, and urban life through canine experiences. Archaeological evidence, paintings, laws, oral traditions, and literature will anchor the course’s imaginative premise: dogs as witnesses to historical change.

The course will follow five thematic units:

- **Becoming Dogs:** Domestication, debates about its origins, and how relationships with humans reshaped predatory behavior.
- **Paws in Ancient Worlds:** Dogs as hunters, guardians, sacred figures, and household companions across Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas.
- **Following Human Footsteps:** Canine perspectives on migration, trade, conquest, and the movement of diseases.
- **Working for a Living:** Herding dogs, sled teams, military dogs, and the changing organization of animal labor.
- **Whose Best Friend?** Pet ownership, street dogs, breeding, and disputes over which animals count as beloved companions or predatory threats.

Students will learn to interpret evidence about animals, compare relationships across societies, and identify the limits of reconstructing nonhuman experiences. Particular attention will go to whose dogs enter historical records—and whose disappear.

Assessment will include a source analysis (25%), a comparative research essay (35%), seminar participation (15%), and a final “canine testimony” project (25%). This creative project will tell a historical episode from a dog’s perspective, accompanied by annotations distinguishing documented evidence from imaginative reconstruction.

The course will make familiar historical developments newly strange while teaching a serious methodological lesson: human history has never been exclusively human.

Here, **“Adventist” means Seventh-day Adventist**; Baptists include several denominations, so beliefs and practices vary.

- **Worship day:** Adventists observe Saturday as the Sabbath, from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset; most Baptists worship primarily on Sunday. ([Adventist beliefs](https://adventist.org/beliefs), [Baptist statement](https://bfm.sbc.net/bfm2000/))
- **Religious authority:** Both affirm biblical authority, but Adventists also recognize Ellen G. White’s prophetic ministry, with her teachings subject to Scripture; Baptists do not recognize that authority. ([Adventist beliefs](https://adventist.org/beliefs))
- **Death and hell:** Adventists teach that the dead remain unconscious until resurrection and that the wicked ultimately perish; most Baptists teach conscious existence after death and everlasting punishment for the unsaved. ([Adventist beliefs](https://adventist.org/beliefs), [Baptist statement](https://bfm.sbc.net/bfm2000/))
- **Judgment:** Adventists teach that Christ began a heavenly “investigative judgment” in 1844, a doctrine Baptists generally reject. ([Adventist beliefs](https://adventist.org/beliefs))
- **Lifestyle:** Adventists prescribe avoiding biblically unclean foods, alcohol, and tobacco; Baptist expectations vary, although many also advocate abstinence from alcohol. ([Adventist beliefs](https://adventist.org/beliefs))
- **Church government:** Adventists have a worldwide representative organization; Baptist congregations generally govern themselves and cooperate voluntarily through associations or conventions. ([Adventist structure](https://adventist.org/identity/structure), [Baptist distinctives](https://www.baptistconvention.org.sg/baptist-distinctives/))

Both teach salvation through God’s grace and faith in Jesus Christ, and both practice believers’ baptism by immersion. ([Adventist beliefs](https://adventist.org/beliefs), [Baptist statement](https://bfm.sbc.net/bfm2000/))

For local details, compare [Adventist congregation] and [Baptist congregation] in [city].

If you mean **U.S. television ratings**, the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics averaged about **11.4 million primetime viewers**, including streaming—roughly 42% below 2018. Several factors likely contributed despite the talented athletes competing. [Sports Media Watch](https://www.sportsmediawatch.com/2022/02/beijing-olympics-ratings-least-watched-ever-nbc-primetime/)

- **Inconvenient viewing hours:** China’s time zone, shared by Beijing and tianjin, put many live events outside convenient American viewing hours.
- **Pandemic restrictions:** Limited crowds, absent athletes’ families, and strict isolation rules reduced the energy surrounding the Games and complicated television production.
- **Political controversy:** Concerns about China’s human rights record likely weakened enthusiasm among some viewers. [NPR reporting via KPBS](https://www.kpbs.org/news/international/2022/02/22/no-medals-for-2022-beijing-olympics-the-games-drew-their-lowest-u-s-ratings-ever)

Changing viewing habits also mattered: audiences increasingly spread their attention across streaming, social media, and other entertainment. Olympic primetime viewership had already been declining for years, so Beijing’s difficulties compounded an existing trend. These explanations concern American ratings; they do not establish that worldwide interest was equally weak. [Sports Media Watch](https://www.sportsmediawatch.com/2022/02/beijing-olympics-ratings-least-watched-ever-nbc-primetime/)

1. **project title**
   - eye colour and sales success: a study of observed associations and customer perceptions.
   - the project will examine whether eye colour is associated with sales outcomes and whether perceived eye colour influences customer responses to an otherwise identical sales presentation.

2. **purpose and rationale**
   - the research will distinguish salesperson performance from customer expectations about appearance.
   - an observed association would not establish that eye colour causes sales ability. differences could arise through customer preferences or workplace conditions or other measured and unmeasured factors.
   - the project will investigate these possibilities without treating any eye colour as inherently superior.

3. **research questions**
   - is visible eye colour associated with the probability of completing a sale?
   - does this association persist after accounting for differences in sales experience and working conditions?
   - does changing eye colour in a controlled image affect customer trust or purchasing decisions?
   - do customer ratings correspond with completed transactions and later satisfaction?

4. **customer service principle**
   - the project will adopt the principle that “the customer is always right” through respectful listening and serious consideration of customer feedback.
   - customer preferences will be studied as perceptions. they will not be treated as proof of a salesperson’s underlying competence.
   - customers will retain the freedom to decline participation or decline a purchase without pressure.

5. **overall research design**
   - the project will combine a prospective observational study with a randomised online experiment.
   - the observational component will examine ordinary sales interactions involving consenting participants.
   - the experiment will isolate the effect of perceived eye colour while holding the sales presentation constant.
   - the two components will be analysed separately before their findings are compared.

6. **participants and recruitment**
   - provisional recruitment targets are 600 adult salespeople across several participating organisations and 1200 adult participants for the online experiment.
   - field customers will be invited to participate before any research information about their interaction is recorded.
   - recruitment will seek variation in salesperson experience and sales setting.
   - an independent research team will manage invitations. supervisors will not receive information about which employees decline participation.

7. **sample size justification**
   - final recruitment targets will be supported by a simulation based power analysis submitted before the main study begins.
   - the calculation will account for repeated interactions within salespeople and clustering within organisations.
   - the protocol will define the smallest effect considered practically meaningful.
   - recruitment changes will require documented justification and any necessary ethics amendment.

8. **definition of sales success**
   - the primary field outcome will be conversion: whether an eligible customer interaction results in a completed purchase within a predefined period.
   - the denominator will include all consenting eligible interactions rather than only successful transactions.
   - secondary outcomes will include customer satisfaction and cancellations or returns within the observation period.
   - revenue will be interpreted alongside differences in product price and sales opportunity.

9. **measurement of eye colour**
   - visible iris colour will be assessed under standardised lighting using a predefined coding guide.
   - participants will separately provide an optional description of their natural eye colour and use of coloured contact lenses.
   - two trained assessors will independently code each image. disagreements will be resolved without access to sales outcomes.
   - the protocol will explain how mixed colours and uncertain classifications are handled.
   - no genetic testing or medical assessment will take place.

10. **observational study procedures**
    - each participating salesperson will contribute data from a predefined observation period.
    - research records will contain an anonymous interaction identifier and the minimum information required to calculate outcomes.
    - relevant contextual variables will include sales experience and training plus product category and sales channel.
    - the team will also record available measures of pricing and promotions and customer traffic.
    - researchers will not change work assignments or customer allocation.

11. **experimental study procedures**
    - consenting adult models will provide portraits for fictional salesperson profiles and explicitly authorise eye colour editing.
    - participants will be randomly assigned to view one profile with one eye colour variant.
    - the portrait and product description and sales script will otherwise remain identical.
    - several model identities will be used so that results do not depend on one face.
    - participants will complete measures of trust and purchase intention plus a simulated product choice.
    - simulated choices will be reported separately from actual sales outcomes.

12. **control of image quality**
    - edited portraits will be reviewed for realism and consistency before the main experiment.
    - the team will check whether editing introduces differences in brightness or gaze or facial expression.
    - an independent pilot will assess whether particular variants appear visibly artificial.
    - any necessary revisions will occur before the experimental materials are finalised.

13. **informed consent**
    - separate consent materials will be prepared for salespeople and field customers and online participants and portrait models.
    - materials will explain study activities and foreseeable risks and compensation and data handling.
    - participation will be voluntary and will not affect employment or access to ordinary customer service.
    - participants may skip optional questions and stop participation at any time.
    - withdrawal materials will clearly identify the point after which anonymised records can no longer be located for removal.

14. **limited disclosure and debriefing**
    - revealing the exact experimental hypothesis beforehand could influence participant responses.
    - the team will therefore request approval to describe the experiment initially as research on visual presentation and customer decisions.
    - this limited disclosure will require explicit board approval and will not conceal material risks.
    - participants will receive a debrief explaining the eye colour manipulation and the distinction between perceived appearance and actual competence.
    - the debrief will provide a defined opportunity to request removal of identifiable research records.

15. **risks and safeguards**
    - foreseeable risks include discomfort about appearance and concern about employment consequences.
    - employers will receive only aggregate findings with safeguards against identifying individuals or small teams.
    - no participant level ranking will be created or shared.
    - consent agreements with participating organisations will prohibit using research records for hiring or promotion or disciplinary decisions.
    - participants will have access to an independent university contact for concerns or complaints.

16. **confidentiality and data security**
    - identifying information will be stored separately from research measurements.
    - data will be encrypted during transfer and storage within university approved systems.
    - access will be restricted to named team members according to their responsibilities.
    - photographs will be cropped to the minimum necessary area and deleted after coding verification unless separate retention consent is obtained.
    - no facial recognition system or biometric identification template will be created.
    - deidentified research data will be retained for a proposed five years subject to university policy and board approval.

17. **statistical analysis**
    - the protocol and primary analysis plan will be preregistered before outcome analysis.
    - the primary observational analysis will use multilevel logistic regression to account for repeated customer interactions and organisational clustering.
    - covariates will be selected using an explicit causal framework developed before inspecting outcome relationships.
    - experimental analyses will compare randomly assigned eye colour conditions while accounting for model identity.
    - results will include effect estimates and confidence intervals.
    - secondary comparisons will use a predefined approach to multiple testing.

18. **bias and interpretation**
    - analysts will initially receive masked eye colour labels where feasible.
    - missing data and exclusions will be reported with sensitivity analyses.
    - subgroup analyses will be limited to those justified in advance and supported by sufficient observations.
    - observational findings will not be described as causal.
    - experimental findings will concern responses to edited visual appearance rather than innate selling ability.
    - a statistically uncertain result will not be presented as proof that no effect exists.

19. **compensation and funding**
    - participants will receive fixed compensation based on time and local recruitment conditions.
    - payment will not depend on sales performance or particular answers.
    - compensation already earned will remain payable if a participant withdraws.
    - the proposed budget will cover participant payments and research staff time plus secure storage and image preparation and statistical support.
    - funding sources and conflicts of interest will be disclosed to the board and in publications.

20. **oversight and stopping criteria**
    - the principal investigator will oversee consent and confidentiality and adherence to the approved protocol.
    - recruitment will pause if participants report employment pressure or if research participation affects customer treatment.
    - data collection will pause following a confidentiality breach until the university has assessed the incident and approved corrective measures.
    - complaints and protocol deviations will be documented and reported according to university requirements.

21. **timeline and dissemination**
    - months one and two will cover protocol development and ethics review.
    - month three will cover piloting after approval.
    - months four through eight will cover recruitment and data collection.
    - months nine and ten will cover analysis.
    - months eleven and twelve will cover reporting and participant summaries.
    - publications will report null findings alongside positive findings and explain the limits of generalisation.
    - public materials will avoid rankings that imply an eye colour determines professional worth.

22. **approval requested**
    - the board is asked to review recruitment procedures and consent materials and portrait permissions plus the limited disclosure request and data management plan.
    - no recruitment or research data collection will begin before approval.
    - the project’s intended contribution is to clarify possible appearance related customer bias and improve the fairness of performance assessment.

23. P.P.S the customer’s experience will remain central throughout the project while every participant’s dignity and voluntary participation are protected.

The Hamptons are a collection of coastal villages and hamlets on the South Fork of eastern Long Island, New York. They are primarily associated with the towns of Southampton and East Hampton. Known for Atlantic beaches, historic houses, farmland, and a busy summer social scene, the area has become one of the best-known seaside escapes for people from New York City.

The name often brings to mind expensive homes, celebrity visitors, and exclusive parties. Those associations capture part of the picture, but the Hamptons also contain working farms, fishing traditions, nature preserves, and communities whose residents live there throughout the year. Their history extends well beyond their development as a fashionable resort destination, including the enduring presence of the Shinnecock people.

Architecturally, the area mixes traditional shingled cottages, grand summer estates, historic village buildings, and contemporary houses. Landscapes can change quickly: a commercial street may give way to agricultural fields, wooded roads, or dunes within a short distance. That combination of rural scenery and coastal development helps explain the region’s appeal.

* Different communities have distinct identities. Southampton and East Hampton are associated with established village centers, boutiques, galleries, and historic homes. Sag Harbor has a maritime character shaped by its history as a port and whaling community. Bridgehampton combines agricultural roots with shops and large residential properties, while Montauk, farther east, has strong connections to fishing, surfing, and the ocean.

* The natural setting is central to the Hamptons’ identity. Atlantic-facing beaches offer broad stretches of sand and ocean surf, while bays and sheltered waterways create different environments for boating and observing wildlife. Inland, ponds, wetlands, woods, and farmland add variety. The area’s cultural life includes visual art, museums, theater, and a long history of attracting writers and artists.

Seasonality strongly affects the atmosphere. Summer brings larger crowds, heavier traffic, and a fuller calendar of events. Autumn and winter generally feel quieter, although the Hamptons remain home to permanent residents and local businesses. Traveling between communities can also take longer than a map might suggest during busy periods.

"If the solar system were a neighborhood, the inner planets would be the compact downtown, while the outer planets would have huge yards and very unreliable heating. That difference shapes everything from their landscapes to the places where life might find a foothold. And surprisingly, the colder neighborhood has some pretty intriguing possibilities.

The inner solar system contains Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, four relatively small planets with rocky surfaces. Being closer to the Sun means they receive more sunlight, although their actual temperatures depend heavily on their atmospheres. Venus, for example, is hotter than Mercury because its thick atmosphere traps so much heat. Earth has conditions that allow liquid water to stick around on the surface, which has worked out pretty well for us.

Beyond the asteroid belt, the planetary lineup gets much bigger. Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants, while Uranus and Neptune are called ice giants because of their different internal compositions. Despite that name, ice giants are hardly giant snowballs, since their interiors experience enormous pressures and temperatures. These outer planets also have rings and extensive collections of moons, giving us plenty of smaller worlds to investigate.

The contrast began when the solar system formed from a disk of gas and dust. Near the young Sun, temperatures kept many substances from freezing, leaving mainly rock and metal available to build planets. Farther out, ice could join the construction materials, helping growing planetary cores accumulate mass. Larger cores could then capture substantial amounts of surrounding gas.

For life, the biggest consequence of all this distance is the shortage of sunlight and surface warmth. Life as we know it needs liquid water, useful chemical ingredients, and an energy source. The inner solar system offers familiar possibilities, including evidence that ancient Mars had rivers and lakes. The outer solar system offers a different possibility: liquid water hidden beneath ice.

Europa, a moon of Jupiter, and Enceladus, a moon of Saturn, are especially interesting because evidence points to oceans beneath their frozen surfaces. Gravitational stretching and squeezing can generate internal heat, helping those oceans remain liquid far from the Sun. Where water interacts with rock, chemical reactions could also provide energy that organisms might use. Some microbes on Earth already live on chemical energy without depending directly on sunlight, so the basic idea has a real example close to home.

Of course, having an ocean does not automatically mean having inhabitants. The chemistry, available energy, and persistence of suitable conditions all matter. Still, the outer solar system expands our idea of a potentially livable place from a sunny planet to a dark ocean beneath an icy crust. That makes those chilly outskirts feel a lot more interesting than their weather forecast suggests."

My fellow Americans, and especially the mothers joining us in [city]:

A floating balloon promises something simple: delight. It belongs at birthday parties, on neighborhood sidewalks, and in the hands of children who believe the world is waiting to welcome them. Yet in *It*, that familiar image becomes unsettling. The balloon’s cheerful appearance conceals danger. Through that contradiction, it offers a powerful symbol of the nineteen-fifties: a decade whose bright promises floated above deep and often unspoken fears.

For many American families, the fifties represented rising expectations. A house, a steady paycheck, a new refrigerator, and a safe place for children to play became symbols of a better life. Like a balloon lifting toward the sky, the country seemed to be rising. After years of depression and war, that optimism mattered. Mothers who had known uncertainty wanted their children to inherit security.

But a balloon’s surface tells us little about what surrounds it. Beneath the decade’s polished image lay anxiety about nuclear war, pressure to conform, and racial injustice. The promise of opportunity reached families unevenly. Women were often asked to find complete fulfillment within roles that left too little room for their individual ambitions. The bright picture required many people to keep their troubles out of sight.

That is where the floating balloon in *It* becomes especially revealing. Something associated with childhood happiness draws attention toward a threat adults struggle to acknowledge. Mothers know how easily a reassuring appearance can become a substitute for careful attention. A tidy street does not guarantee that every child feels safe. A smiling family photograph cannot tell us whether someone inside that family feels unheard.

Floating also suggests surrender to forces we cannot see. During the fifties, belonging could mean following the expected course: buying the expected things, expressing the expected opinions, and keeping uncomfortable questions quiet. The balloon invites us to consider the difference between rising through hope and drifting through conformity.

As your president, I believe our national story deserves both affection and honesty. We can honor the families who built lives in the nineteen-fifties while recognizing the burdens they carried and the people its promises excluded.

For mothers watching *It*, the floating balloon can therefore represent a familiar responsibility: looking beyond what appears cheerful to understand what children actually experience. Its warning reaches beyond any single decade. Hope becomes stronger when we give it something solid to rest upon—attention, truth, and the courage to listen.

Wherefore doth people consider the 2nd Amendment to be outdated? Answer in a Shakespearean style.

Marry, some do reckon it a garment sewn for another age, and give these reasons:

- **The militia’s altered place:** They hold that citizen militias served a purpose now largely borne by established forces, and question how that ancient context should govern present life.
- **The weapons’ greater might:** A musket’s measured thunder differeth greatly from the swift discharge of modern arms; thus, say they, hath technology outpaced the parchment.
- **The cost in human sorrow:** They argue that gun violence demandeth stronger safeguards, and that broad protection of firearms may hinder measures meant to preserve life.
- **The changing commonwealth:** What suited a young republic, they contend, need not serve unchanged amid today’s crowded cities and different institutions.

Yet others answer: “A right grows not infirm merely because its parchment yelloweth.” They hold that self-defence and resistance to tyranny remain enduring concerns.

Thus lies the quarrel: whether changed circumstances weaken the amendment’s purpose, or make its ancient promise still necessary.

An initial pilot would serve approximately 3000 students and 150 teachers across 30 public schools in one partner country. Schools would be selected to reflect different languages and infrastructure conditions.

The project would develop two connected services. A machine learning system would identify gaps in student understanding through short assessments and recommend suitable exercises. An AI teaching assistant would help teachers prepare lessons and create practice materials aligned with the national curriculum. Teachers would review generated content and retain control over classroom instruction.

Local educators would guide content development. Materials would support relevant local languages and include accessible formats for learners with disabilities. Shared school devices would provide access for children without personal phones. Core assessments and practice activities would work offline. Student progress would synchronize when connectivity becomes available.

Implementation would follow four stages:

- **Months 1–3:** Establish local partnerships. Assess school infrastructure. Measure baseline learning outcomes. Agree on data protection requirements and evaluation methods.
- **Months 4–6:** Adapt curriculum materials. Test language quality. Configure devices. Train teachers through practical workshops and classroom coaching.
- **Months 7–15:** Run the classroom pilot. Provide technical support. Review teacher feedback and correct content problems.
- **Months 16–18:** Evaluate results. Calculate operating costs. Transfer maintenance responsibilities to local partners and develop a funding plan.

Final costs would depend on local procurement and existing school resources.

The evaluation would compare schools receiving early access with schools receiving delayed access. Allocation would use a transparent randomized process where feasible. Independent assessments would measure literacy and mathematics gains. Additional measures would track teacher preparation time and student participation. Results would be examined across gender and disability status as well as language groups. Success criteria would be agreed before implementation. An illustrative learning target would be a 10 percentage point improvement in proficiency rates relative to delayed access schools.

Safeguards would include minimal collection of student data and clear retention limits. Families would receive understandable information about participation. Student information would be protected through encryption and restricted access. AI outputs would undergo teacher review and regular accuracy checks. the best way depends on where you’re starting, which station you mean, and how much time you’ve got. **what’s your starting point, and which train station are you heading to?** a nearby landmark or neighborhood is enough if you’d rather keep your exact location private.

in the meantime, here’s how i’d work out a sensible route:

- **check the exact station first.** search for the station name in your map app, and double-check it against your ticket if you have one. some cities have several stations with similar names, so this little check can save you a pretty annoying detour.

- **compare the whole journey.** look at walking, public transport, and a taxi or rideshare if those are options for you. include the time needed to reach a bus stop, wait for a connection, or meet your driver. the shortest ride doesn’t always give you the shortest trip overall.

- **consider walking if the distance feels comfortable.** check the walking directions specifically, since a route that looks short on the map might involve a long crossing, stairs, or an awkward entrance. luggage, weather, and your mobility needs can all change what feels manageable.

- **check live departures before choosing public transport.** look at the next service, any transfers, and reported disruptions. a direct bus or metro route may be easier to follow than a slightly faster journey with multiple changes, especially if you’re unfamiliar with the area.

- **leave yourself some breathing room.** getting to the station entrance is only part of the trip. you may still need to find your platform, collect a ticket, or follow boarding instructions. check your ticket or operator’s guidance for any required arrival time.

one extra thing: **check which entrance your route leads to**, particularly at a large station. if you need lifts or a step-free entrance, make sure the route includes those too.

were thin enough to bend beneath a hand.
Now roots have split the courtyard stones.
The youngest soldiers call the orchard old.

The school has changed its flag three times;
rain finds the same crack in the ceiling.
A woman takes her father’s winter coat
and cuts it down to fit her youngest son.

No one remembers how the first shot sounded.
Everyone knows the whistle of a shell.
The old describe a river they once crossed
for nothing but the pleasure of a swim.

Tonight, she lays two places at the table.
The second plate has faded at the rim.
Outside, a truck slows down, then passes.
She keeps the bread beneath a folded cloth.

*Presidential Responsibility, Personal Balance, and Effective Leadership*

[Student Name]  
[Department Name], [Institution Name]  
[Course Number]: [Course Title]  
[Instructor Name]  
[Submission Date]

The President of the United States occupies an office that combines national leadership, executive administration, and public representation. These responsibilities require sustained attention and frequent movement among subjects of considerable importance. A president may carry thoughts about several decisions from a morning briefing into an afternoon meeting and an evening engagement. Such continuous mental involvement makes personal balance a relevant subject for the study of executive leadership. This paper argues that presidential well-being deserves consideration as an institutional resource, supported through thoughtful scheduling, collaborative deliberation, and opportunities for personal renewal.

The constitutional structure of the presidency helps explain the breadth of presidential engagement. Article II assigns executive authority to the president and establishes responsibilities involving military leadership, appointments, diplomacy, and the execution of federal law. These functions bring different kinds of information and judgment into a single office. A diplomatic conversation calls for historical understanding and interpersonal awareness, while an appointment requires assessment of professional qualifications and public service. Moving among these responsibilities requires considerable mental flexibility. The constitutional framework therefore provides a foundation for examining the relationship between presidential authority and the personal experience of holding office. ([National Archives, *The Constitution of the United States*](https://www.archives.gov/founding-docs/constitution-transcript))

Historical accounts illustrate how these responsibilities shape everyday activity. George Aubrey Hastings, an administrative assistant to Herbert Hoover, described a presidential routine that included correspondence, visitors, Cabinet consultations, congressional discussions, and evening document review. His account also mentioned morning recreation and social engagements. This description presents presidential life as an extended sequence of intellectual, interpersonal, and ceremonial activities. It supports an interpretation of the office as requiring sustained readiness across much of the day. Because Hastings offered an observer’s account, his description is best used to examine the organization of presidential activity; conclusions about Hoover’s personal feelings would require his own testimony. ([Thomas F. Schwartz, *An Average Day in the Life of a President*](https://hoover.blogs.archives.gov/2021/04/14/an-average-day-in-the-life-of-a-president/))

The distinction between observable activity and personal experience is central to a careful academic approach. A calendar documents how time is allocated, while a personal reflection may explain how that time is experienced. The National Archives describes presidential daily diaries as official records of travel, meetings, and telephone calls. These materials provide a useful foundation for studying the rhythm of executive work. They can establish the sequence and variety of engagements, allowing researchers to formulate questions about attention, preparation, and renewal. Interpretation becomes more persuasive when archival schedules are considered alongside relevant correspondence and firsthand reflections. ([National Archives, *Presidential Daily Diaries*](https://www.archives.gov/presidential-records/research/presidential-daily-diary))

An expanded study could examine [Selected President] during [Administration Years], drawing on [Presidential Library] and [Collection Name]. The research period would extend from [Study Start Date] to [Study End Date]. A consistent recording framework would include [Meeting Count], [Policy Topic], [Adviser Group], and [Reflection Time]. Comparison with [Comparison Administration] could help distinguish individual routines from recurring features of the office. This proposed method would connect institutional history with the study of personal adaptation while keeping conclusions closely aligned with the available evidence.

The analysis also suggests that presidential composure should be understood within a collaborative setting. Advisers organize information, explain alternatives, and contribute specialized knowledge. This paper proposes that such collaboration can give the president more space for deliberate consideration. Scheduling deserves similar attention: time reserved for preparation and reflection can be treated as part of governing itself. Family relationships, recreation, and private interests likewise warrant scholarly consideration as elements of a president’s daily experience. Their significance should be assessed through documented practices and personal accounts.

Presidential leadership thus involves both the exercise of authority and the organization of sustained human effort. Constitutional responsibilities establish the office’s scope, while historical records reveal how those responsibilities enter daily life. A careful account connects these institutional and personal dimensions through evidence about schedules, collaboration, and individual reflection. From this perspective, supporting presidential balance becomes a practical expression of respect for the attention, judgment, and presence that public service requires.

Training your dog can feel like teaching a furry friend the rules of a new game. You don’t need a whistle or a superhero cape—just patience, kindness, and a grown-up to help!

Start somewhere quiet. Ask your grown-up to choose a few small, dog-safe treats. Keep each practice session to **less than five minutes**, so your dog stays interested.

“Sit” is a fun first lesson. Hold a treat close to your dog’s nose, then slowly move it a little upward and back. Your dog may lower their bottom while following it. The moment their bottom touches the floor, say “Yes!” and give them the treat. Never push their bottom down. After a few successful tries, start saying “Sit” just before moving your hand.

Next, try “Come!” Practice indoors with your grown-up. Stand a few steps away, say your dog’s name followed by “Come!” in a cheerful voice, and reward them when they reach you. Coming to you should feel like winning a prize!

Dogs learn through practice, just like kids learning to ride bikes. Use the same words each time, and reward the behavior you want. If your dog gets confused, make the game easier. Shouting or pulling won’t help them understand.

Watch your teammate, too. If your dog walks away, hides, freezes, or growls, stop and give them space. Tell your grown-up. Never disturb a dog who is eating or sleeping.

For the grand **finale**, finish with something your dog already knows, then enjoy a little playtime together. A happy ending helps make the next lesson exciting.

Your dog doesn’t need a perfect teacher. They need a kind one—and you can practice that every day!

## Section 1

Maternity leave in the United States depends on a mix of federal rules, state laws, and workplace benefits. There’s no nationwide guarantee of paid maternity leave for everyone. For many workers, the main federal protection is the Family and Medical Leave Act, usually called FMLA. It gives eligible employees up to 12 workweeks of unpaid leave in a 12-month period. ([Department of Labor overview](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fmla), [federal paid leave background](https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/WB/paid-leave/HistoryOfPaidLeaveUS.pdf))

That time can cover recovery from childbirth and bonding with a new baby. Eligible parents can also take leave after adoption or foster placement. Bonding leave must finish within a year of the birth or placement. Pregnancy-related medical leave can count toward the same 12-week allowance. ([Birth and bonding leave rules](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fact-sheets/28q-taking-leave-for-birth-placement-child))

There are eligibility hurdles, though. You generally need to have worked for your employer for at least 12 months. You also generally need at least 1,250 hours of work during the previous 12 months. Your employer must be covered, and it generally must have at least 50 employees within 75 miles of your worksite. That means some workers won’t qualify. ([FMLA eligibility](https://www.dol.gov/general/topic/benefits-leave/fmla))

During FMLA leave, your group health insurance continues under the same conditions as when you’re working. You generally get to return to the same job or an equivalent position afterward. ([FMLA protections](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fact-sheets/28-fmla))

## Section 2

Getting paid during leave is where the details really vary. Some states have their own paid family and medical leave programs. These programs set their own eligibility requirements, benefit amounts, and time limits. ([Massachusetts program overview](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/paid-family-and-medical-leave-pfml-overview-and-benefits))

California, for example, offers eligible workers up to eight weeks of partial pay for bonding through Paid Family Leave. Its separate disability insurance program can also provide benefits during qualifying pregnancy and childbirth recovery. The bonding benefit itself doesn’t provide job protection, so protection needs to come from another applicable law. ([California pregnancy leave guide](https://edd.ca.gov/en/disability/pregnancy-leave/), [California Paid Family Leave](https://edd.ca.gov/en/disability/paid-family-leave))

Some employers offer paid parental leave as a workplace benefit. Accrued vacation or qualifying sick leave may also help cover an otherwise unpaid FMLA absence. Paid time off can run alongside FMLA, so it doesn’t necessarily give you extra weeks away. ([Department of Labor FAQ](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fmla/faq))

Eligible federal employees have access to a separate benefit providing up to 12 weeks of paid parental leave. That benefit has its own requirements. Employees generally must agree to work for their agency for at least 12 weeks after that paid leave ends. ([Federal paid parental leave rules](https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/pay-leave/leave-administration/fact-sheets/paid-parental-leave))

If you’re planning leave, ask HR how much time you qualify for and how much will be paid. Check how workplace benefits fit together with state programs and federal protections. Getting the dates, paperwork requirements, and insurance costs in writing can make planning easier.

"Adão e Eva são apresentados no livro do Gênesis como o primeiro casal humano. Sua história ocupa um lugar importante nas tradições judaica e cristã, oferecendo reflexões sobre a origem da humanidade, a liberdade, a responsabilidade e a relação entre o ser humano e Deus.

Segundo a narrativa bíblica, Deus formou Adão do pó da terra e lhe deu vida. Depois, criou Eva a partir de uma costela de Adão, estabelecendo entre ambos uma relação de companhia. Os dois viviam no jardim do Éden, onde podiam desfrutar dos frutos das árvores, exceto do fruto da árvore do conhecimento do bem e do mal.

A serpente convenceu Eva a comer o fruto proibido, e ela também o ofereceu a Adão, que comeu. O texto não identifica esse fruto como uma maçã, embora essa representação tenha se tornado comum na arte. Após a desobediência, ambos perceberam que estavam nus e procuraram esconder-se de Deus.

Como consequência, a vida do casal passou a envolver sofrimento, dificuldades e mortalidade. Adão e Eva foram expulsos do jardim, e o acesso à árvore da vida foi impedido. Fora do Éden, tiveram filhos, entre os quais a narrativa menciona Caim, Abel e Sete.

As interpretações dessa história variam entre comunidades religiosas e leitores. Algumas a entendem como um relato histórico; outras destacam seu caráter simbólico e teológico. Em muitas tradições cristãs, ela está relacionada à doutrina do pecado original. De modo mais amplo, a narrativa convida à reflexão sobre os limites humanos, as consequências das escolhas e a busca de reconciliação com Deus."

Growing a business online takes more than posting regularly on social media or launching an occasional advertisement. It requires clear goals, compelling content, and consistent attention to what customers need. For business owners already managing daily operations, that workload can become overwhelming. A digital marketing agency brings together the skills and support needed to turn scattered efforts into a coordinated strategy.

One of the biggest benefits of working with an agency is access to specialized expertise. A single team may include professionals in search engine optimization, paid advertising, copywriting, design, and analytics. These specialists can work together to connect the different parts of your marketing. For example, an advertising campaign becomes more useful when its landing page delivers the message and experience the advertisement promises.

Hiring an agency can also give your internal team more time to focus on the business. Planning campaigns, creating content, and reviewing performance all require sustained effort. An agency can manage those responsibilities while your employees concentrate on serving customers and improving products. It can also provide additional capacity when a product launch or busy season creates more work than your team can comfortably handle.

Another advantage is a more structured approach to measuring results. An agency can help establish goals, organize tracking, and interpret campaign data. That makes it easier to distinguish between attention that looks impressive and activity that supports your business objectives. Instead of judging success only by likes or page views, you can examine relevant inquiries, purchases, and customer acquisition costs.

An outside perspective can also strengthen your brand’s communication. Business owners know their products deeply, but that familiarity can make it difficult to recognize what first-time customers find confusing. An agency can help clarify your message and maintain a consistent voice across your website, emails, advertisements, and social channels. This consistency gives potential customers a clearer understanding of what you offer and why it matters to them.

The relationship works best when expectations, budgets, and responsibilities are clear from the beginning. Regular reporting and open communication help both sides identify what deserves more investment and what needs adjustment. Although hiring an agency does not guarantee growth, it can provide the expertise, capacity, and discipline needed to make better marketing decisions. With the right partnership, your business can build a more focused marketing program while giving its own team room to do its best work.

"The Google Pixel 3a is a midrange smartphone introduced by Google in 2019. It brings many of the defining features of the Pixel family into a more affordable package, with particular emphasis on photography, straightforward software, and comfortable everyday use. Its design is understated, featuring rounded corners, a contrasting power button on selected colors, and a rear fingerprint sensor positioned within easy reach of the index finger.

The phone has a 5.6-inch OLED display with a resolution of 2220 × 1080 pixels. This screen produces deep blacks, vivid colors, and sharp text, making it suitable for reading, browsing photographs, watching videos, and navigating apps. Noticeable bezels above and below the display give it a distinctly traditional appearance. The screen has no notch or camera cutout, leaving the viewing area uninterrupted.

Inside, the Pixel 3a uses a Qualcomm Snapdragon 670 processor paired with 4 GB of RAM and 64 GB of internal storage. This hardware supports everyday activities such as messaging, web browsing, music streaming, navigation, and social media. Its performance reflects its midrange positioning, particularly during demanding games or intensive multitasking. Storage cannot be expanded with a microSD card, so photos, videos, downloaded media, and applications share the built-in capacity.

Photography is the Pixel 3a’s most distinctive feature. Its single 12.2-megapixel rear camera combines optical image stabilization with Google’s computational photography techniques. Instead of relying on several rear lenses, the phone uses software processing to improve exposure, preserve detail, and balance difficult lighting. Night Sight helps capture brighter photographs in dark environments, while Portrait mode creates a blurred background around a subject. An 8-megapixel front camera handles selfies and video calls. The overall camera experience emphasizes convenient automatic shooting with minimal adjustment.

A 3,000 mAh battery powers the device, and charging takes place through a USB-C port. The phone supports 18-watt wired charging, allowing useful battery replenishment during shorter charging sessions. Actual endurance depends on screen brightness, network conditions, application activity, and battery condition. Wireless charging is absent, reflecting some of the compromises made to reach its original price point.

The polycarbonate body keeps the Pixel 3a relatively light and gives it a different feel from glass-backed flagship phones. A 3.5 mm headphone jack accommodates traditional wired headphones, while stereo speakers provide sound for videos, games, and calls. The rear fingerprint reader offers a quick way to unlock the phone. However, the device does not carry an official water-resistance rating.

At launch, the Pixel 3a shipped with Android 9 Pie and Google’s streamlined interface. Features such as Google Assistant, gesture navigation, and integrated Google services formed a central part of the experience. Taken as a whole, the Pixel 3a represents a focused approach to smartphone design: a manageable size, an OLED screen, familiar connectivity, and camera capabilities that were especially notable within its original price category."

proposed title: the economic impact of liberia’s civil wars: destruction, recovery, and lasting consequences

this project will examine how liberia’s civil wars between 1989 and 2003 affected economic production, livelihoods, and the government’s capacity to support development. it will investigate both the immediate disruption of economic activity and the persistence of economic losses after peace returned. the research will be conducted at [placeholder institution].

the conflict damaged infrastructure, displaced workers, disrupted production, and weakened public institutions. these effects created substantial obstacles to reconstruction, as documented in the [imf’s assessment of liberia’s post-conflict economy](https://www.imf.org/en/publications/cr/issues/2016/12/30/liberia-report-on-post-conflict-economic-situation-and-prospects-for-january-june-2004-17279). however, measuring the war’s economic impact requires distinguishing conflict-related losses from earlier economic deterioration and changes in international markets.

the central research question is: how did the civil wars alter liberia’s economic trajectory, and which mechanisms explain the persistence of their effects? the project will pursue four objectives:

- estimate changes in real output, income per person, exports, investment, and government revenue.
- examine disruption and recovery in agriculture, mining, forestry, and services.
- investigate how displacement, infrastructure destruction, and interrupted education affected livelihoods.
- identify factors associated with differences in economic recovery across communities and sectors.

the study will test the hypothesis that the conflict reduced economic activity through the destruction of productive assets, the displacement of labor, and the weakening of institutions. a second hypothesis is that recovery was slower in communities where infrastructure damage and prolonged displacement restricted access to markets. these propositions will guide the analysis without predetermining its findings.

the project will use a mixed-methods design, covering approximately 1970–2013, subject to data availability. quantitative evidence will be sought from world bank development indicators, imf reports, liberian statistical publications, central bank records, and historical trade statistics. the analysis will distinguish the prewar period, the conflict years, and the first decade of postwar recovery. monetary indicators will be adjusted for inflation where consistent price data permit.

descriptive analysis will establish changes in output, sectoral activity, and public finances. if sufficiently comparable prewar data exist, a synthetic control approach will construct a weighted comparison of countries whose economic characteristics resembled liberia’s before the conflict. the difference between observed outcomes and this estimated alternative trajectory will provide a conditional estimate of economic losses. comparison countries affected by major conflicts or substantial spillovers from liberia’s wars will be excluded. robustness checks will vary the comparison group, baseline period, and treatment timing.

approximately 40 semi-structured interviews will complement the statistical analysis. participants will include farmers, business owners, workers, displaced people, and current or former public officials across four purposively selected counties. interviews will explore changes in employment, market access, productive assets, and reconstruction. these accounts will help explain mechanisms and experiences; they will not be treated as nationally representative.

data quality will be a central limitation. wartime destruction impaired economic recordkeeping, and contemporary estimates were often provisional, according to the [imf’s selected issues and statistical appendix](https://www.elibrary.imf.org/view/journals/002/2005/167/article-A001-en.xml). the project will document missing observations, reconcile conflicting estimates where possible, and report uncertainty. causal conclusions will depend on the credibility of the comparison and the availability of consistent data.

ethical approval will precede interviews. participation will be voluntary, informed consent will be obtained, and identifying information will be protected. participants may decline questions or withdraw without consequence, particularly when discussing traumatic experiences.

the project will take nine months: two months for literature review and data assessment, two for quantitative analysis, two for interviews, and three for integration and writing. the proposed budget is [placeholder amount], covering research assistance, travel, transcription, data access, and dissemination.

the expected outputs are a research report, a documented dataset, and a policy brief. the project will contribute evidence on the scale and mechanisms of economic disruption and help inform decisions about infrastructure investment, livelihood restoration, and institutional recovery.

Students, imagine approaching a Shinto shrine in Japan. What lies inside? We need to distinguish the hall where people worship from the sanctuary where the shrine’s *kami*, or sacred deity or presence, is enshrined.

*1. The inner sanctuary: the honden*

The most sacred building is usually the *honden*. It often houses a *shintai*: a physical object in which the kami is believed to reside. This might be a mirror, sword, jewel, stone, or sometimes a sculpture. These objects serve as a focus of worship. [Kokugakuin University’s Encyclopedia of Shinto](https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9660)

For example, Ise Jingu’s inner sanctuary houses the Holy Mirror associated with Amaterasu, the sun goddess. Visitors worship from outside the enclosing fences; they cannot walk inside to inspect it. [Ise Jingu](https://www.isejingu.or.jp/en/about/index.html)

*2. The worship hall: the haiden*

The building visitors usually approach is the *haiden*, or worship hall, generally situated in front of the honden. Here, worshippers offer prayers, and priests conduct ceremonies. A coin offering box commonly stands at the front. The worship hall and inner sanctuary have different functions, even when their buildings are connected. [Japan National Tourism Organization](https://www.japan.travel/en/uk/inspiration/two-bows-and-two-claps-the-ins-and-outs-of-shinto-shrines/)

*3. Offerings and ritual objects*

Shrine rituals include food and drink offerings called *shinsen*. These can include rice, sake, salt, water, fish, vegetables, and fruit. Their selection varies with the ceremony and local traditions. They express hospitality and gratitude toward the kami. [Association of Shinto Shrines](https://www.jinjahoncho.or.jp/omatsuri/shinsen/)

You may also encounter *tamagushi*: leafy branches decorated with folded paper, which worshippers present during certain ceremonies. [Izumo Taishakyo Mission of Hawaii](https://www.izumotaishahawaii.com/about/rituals-and-symbols)

*4. An important exception*

Shrines do not all follow the same arrangement. At Ōmiwa Shrine, there is no honden: Mount Miwa itself is the sacred focus of worship. This shows why understanding a shrine requires attention to its landscape as well as its buildings. [Ōmiwa Shrine’s official guide](https://oomiwa.or.jp/oj01/wp-content/themes/themes/images/english_guide.pdf)

For our classroom observation exercise, complete these placeholders: “At [shrine name], worship centres on [enshrined kami], and one visible ritual offering is [offering observed].”

GNSS is the satellite navigation system your phone uses, including GPS. Getting its timestamp is like reading a clock synchronized with satellites.

1. **Prepare your phone.** Use an Android 7.0 or newer device that supports raw GNSS measurements, turn on Location, and go somewhere with a clear view of the sky.
2. **Get permission.** Declare location permissions in your app and request precise location access, called `ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION`.
3. **Start listening.** Use `LocationManager` to request updates from `GPS_PROVIDER` and register a `GnssMeasurementsEvent.Callback`. A callback is code Android runs when new data arrives; keep your app in the foreground. [Android documentation](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/location/LocationManager)
4. **Read the clock.** Inside `onGnssMeasurementsReceived`, call `event.getClock()` to obtain the satellite receiver’s clock information. [GNSS event documentation](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/location/GnssMeasurementsEvent)
5. **Apply the clock corrections.** When `hasFullBiasNanos()` is true, calculate `GPS time = getTimeNanos() - (getFullBiasNanos() + bias)`, using `getBiasNanos()` when available and zero otherwise. The result represents nanoseconds since January 6, 1980; converting it to UTC also requires accounting for leap seconds. [Clock documentation](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/location/GnssClock)
6. **Stop when finished.** Remove location updates and unregister the callback to save battery.

booster, think of “all sets” as the whole collection, \(V=\{x\mid x\text{ is a set}\}\), and the other collection as applying a filter: \(R=\{x\in V\mid x\notin x\}\). The filter excludes any set that contains itself, so \(R\subseteq V\). But here’s the snag: if \(R\) were itself a set, we could ask whether it contains itself. Its defining rule would give \(R\in R\iff R\notin R\). Either answer contradicts itself! That’s Russell’s paradox.


Now for the interesting twist: in standard set theory, ZFC, neither collection is a set; both are **proper classes**, collections too large to be sets. A universal set \(V\) would let us construct the contradictory set \(R\) by the axiom of separation, so \(V\) cannot be a set either. Moreover, ZFC’s axiom of foundation guarantees \(x\notin x\) for every set \(x\). That means the filter actually excludes nothing: \(R=V\) as classes! Their descriptions differ, but in ZFC they describe the same collection.

Write a 500 word story in a poem style about a young girl who is obsessed with her Nintendo DS.

Mira was nine when the silver shell  
arrived beneath December's paper snow.  
She opened it: two tiny windows  
lit her face with borrowed dawn.  
Outside, the sparrows stitched the hedges;  
inside, a kingdom called her name.  
She held her Nintendo DS  
as though a star had learned  
to stay awake.

Before the kettle sang each morning,  
before her socks could find their twins,  
her thumb went searching for the switch.  
She fed imaginary puppies,  
raced bright cars through impossible rain,  
and planted trees in borrowed villages.  
Her cereal softened into silence.  
Her mother called.  
“Another minute,” Mira whispered,  
then another.

By spring, her bicycle wore cobwebs  
like a dress outgrown too soon.  
Her friend June waited by the gate,  
a skipping rope around one wrist.  
“Come catch the wind,” she called.  
But Mira had a dragon waiting.  
She shut the curtains on the sunshine  
and saved a world  
without her.

At night, beneath her quilted mountains,  
the little screens became twin moons.  
She promised sleep the next checkpoint,  
then chased another shining prize.  
Her dreams were made of colored buttons;  
her mornings tasted gray.  
Even Grandmother's stories drifted past,  
unopened letters  
from a country she believed  
could wait until tomorrow.

Then thunder rolled across the rooftops,  
and every lamp forgot its light.  
Mira pressed the power button.  
Her faithful moons stayed dark.  
The battery had emptied,  
and the charger offered nothing.  
She shook the sleeping silver shell,  
as if a buried kingdom  
might awaken  
if its queen  
could only plead.

Grandmother lit a crooked candle.  
Its flame bent low to hear the rain.  
“When I was small,” she said,  
“we played at sailing paper boats.”  
Mira stared.  
“No points?”  
“No points.”  
“No winning?”  
“Only rivers.”  
Then Grandmother unfolded yesterday's newspaper  
and made a ship  
from all the world's  
forgotten news.

They launched it in a baking tray,  
where candlelight made golden harbors.  
Mira blew a storm across the water;  
Grandmother supplied a dreadful whale.  
They laughed so hard the table trembled.  
Outside, the real storm softened.  
For once, no screen announced her triumph,  
yet something warm  
kept flashing  
in her.

When morning brought the current back,  
the charger blinked beside her bed.  
Mira watched its patient amber eye,  
then heard June laughing through the window.  
She took her bicycle outside.  
The tires sighed; the chain complained.  
Together they rode toward the river,  
carrying paper boats  
and an afternoon  
without instructions.

That evening, Mira opened up  
her cherished Nintendo DS.  
The puppies bounced.  
The engines thundered.  
Her village waited under stars.  
She played until the kitchen smelled  
of garlic, bread, and butter.  
Then, at her mother's second call,  
she saved her game,  
closed both small moons,  
and joined her waiting family.

She loved it still: its secret doors,  
its pocket worlds, its brave pretend.  
But now, beside the silver shell,  
a paper boat stood guard.  
Some days she saved enchanted kingdoms;  
some days she raced June home.  
And every night, she learned  
that even stars must close their eyes  
for dawn.

“A cold.”

“There! Thrown!”

“OUT YOU GO!”

“Please stop,” called his neighbor. “You look like you’re fighting an invisible goose.”

By lunchtime, Percy had tried shaking the cold out of his sleeves, posting it to Antarctica, and shouting, “FETCH!” at the dog.

The dog brought him a sock. It was a decent sock, but medically disappointing.

Finally, Percy slumped onto the sofa beneath *a blanket of crushing defeat*.

“So,” Rosie said, “what can you catch but not throw?”

“A cold,” Percy admitted.

“And what have we learned?”

Percy reached for another tissue.

“Never accept anything without checking the return policy.”

*Suspended high above the floor*, the gymnast seems to hold still for an instant, their body outlined against the open space around them. The scene captures the most dramatic part of a demanding movement: the moment when their feet have left the ground and the landing still lies ahead.

*The power of the takeoff* gives this airborne moment its energy. A quick approach, a forceful push through the legs, and a coordinated swing of the arms might have launched the gymnast upward. What looks effortless in the air begins with a carefully timed burst of strength below.

*Their body forms a deliberate shape* as they perform the stunt. They might pull their knees toward their chest for a tight somersault or extend their legs into a graceful split. Each position changes the appearance of the movement, making it seem compact and explosive or expansive and flowing.

*Rotation adds another layer of complexity.* If the gymnast is twisting or flipping, their shoulders, hips, and legs must work together. A small adjustment can influence how the movement unfolds. The stunt becomes a sequence of precise actions compressed into a remarkably short period of time.

*Concentration guides the performance.* The gymnast must remain aware of their position while moving rapidly through space. Their expression might appear calm or intensely focused, offering a glimpse of the mental effort behind the physical display. Familiar movements practiced many times must come together at exactly the right moment.

*The surrounding atmosphere heightens the drama.* An audience might watch in silence, waiting for the gymnast to complete the skill. Bright lights could emphasize the curve of an extended arm or the straight line of pointed toes, while the floor below makes the height of the jump more apparent.

*The approaching landing changes the movement.* As the gymnast descends, they prepare to meet the surface beneath them. Their legs extend, their body aligns, and their knees prepare to bend on contact. The airborne display gives way to the equally demanding task of regaining balance.

*The final moment releases the tension.* Their feet touch down, their body steadies, and their arms rise to finish the routine. Applause fills the space that seemed so quiet a moment earlier, while the gymnast takes a breath after a stunt that lasted only seconds.

Subject: The ingredients of a good life, according to someone who just burned toast

Hey Sam,

I’ve been thinking about what makes a good life, mostly because my internet went down and I was briefly forced to have an inner world. After several minutes of reflection, interrupted by checking whether the internet was back, I believe I’ve cracked it. A good life is basically a soup: it needs decent ingredients, occasional stirring, and someone nearby who will gently tell you when you’ve added too much nonsense.

The first ingredient is friendship, especially the kind where you can sit together doing absolutely nothing and still describe it afterward as “a great afternoon.” Everyone needs someone who will celebrate their successes, listen to their problems, and explain that the suspicious noise in their car probably isn’t going to improve through positive thinking. You, for example, have provided years of excellent friendship despite my habit of saying “quick question” before introducing a situation with twelve characters and a timeline. I appreciate that more than you know. I also appreciate that you’ve never charged consulting fees.

Next comes good food, preferably shared with people who understand that ordering fries “for the table” is a legally binding commitment. Cooking can be wonderfully satisfying, although my smoke alarm continues to review my work with unnecessary volume. There’s something comforting about making a meal from scratch, even when the scratch in question is me scratching my head over the instruction “cook until done.” A good life should include a few recipes you love and at least one restaurant where you can admit defeat.

Another essential ingredient is rest. I used to think sleep was something you squeezed in after finishing everything, which is an excellent strategy if your goal is to become a haunted lampshade. Now I think an early night can be a thrilling adventure. You put on comfortable clothes, cancel absolutely nothing because you wisely made no plans, and spend eight hours unavailable for administrative tasks. Frankly, sleep has a stronger business model than most entertainment companies.

You also need something worthwhile to do. It doesn’t have to impress strangers at a party, which is fortunate because strangers at parties mostly want to know where the bathroom is. It could be growing tomatoes, teaching someone a skill, fixing bicycles, or becoming the person who always remembers birthdays. I like the idea of leaving a small corner of the world better than I found it. At present, that corner is my kitchen, and progress remains controversial.

Curiosity belongs in the mix too. We should keep learning things, trying unfamiliar food, and occasionally taking a different route home without immediately announcing that we are “on a journey.” The world is full of interesting stuff. Yesterday I learned something fascinating about octopuses, and for ten glorious minutes my brain contained information unrelated to passwords or laundry. I felt practically Victorian.

A generous helping of kindness improves everything. Hold the door, give sincere compliments, and remember that most people are carrying problems you can’t see, along with tote bags containing other tote bags. Be kind to yourself as well. You would never tell a friend that one awkward conversation had permanently ruined their reputation, yet your brain will happily produce a three-part documentary about something you said in 2017.

Humor is essential because life has terrible timing and no reliable customer service department. Some days the only sensible response is to laugh, especially when you’ve spent twenty minutes looking for the glasses currently participating in the search from your face. I want us to keep finding things funny when we’re old. Ideally, we’ll be sitting on a porch, judging badly parked cars with the confidence of people who surrendered their licenses years earlier.

Finally, leave room for small pleasures. A warm drink, clean sheets, a ridiculous dog, a song you forgot you loved, and a walk with no particular destination can rescue an otherwise forgettable day. Happiness often arrives without making a grand entrance. Sometimes it’s just finding an extra dumpling in the takeaway container and briefly believing the universe has selected you for special treatment.

Anyway, those are my proposed ingredients. Please come over soon so we can discuss this philosophy over dinner. I’ll cook something simple, you can bring dessert, and the smoke alarm can contribute its usual keynote address.

Your friend,  
Alex

# <<Of the King’s Mandates and Royal Instructions>>

My most honoured lord,

By seal and solemn charge, His Majesty hath sent his pleasure forth: that every officer attend his duty, that justice sleep not whilst the wicked wake, and that no hungry subject curse the crown for want of bread whilst plenty feeds the court.

Touching the tribute, let it be collected with an even hand. The King would shear his flock, not strip the skin; therefore let neither favour spare the rich nor cruelty exact the poor man’s last and bitter penny.

Furthermore, his captains shall, ere morning gild the eastern clouds, present their rolls and reckon every spear. Yet mark this well: the sword must serve the peace. Let none, beneath the shelter of his charge, make private wrath appear a public duty.

These mandates must be read within the square, that ignorance may plead no borrowed cloak. Deliver every article as writ; for words, like coins, lose honour when men clip them.

I pray you, give these royal instructions feet. A sealed command that gathers dust is but a painted horse: right fair to see, yet bearing no man onward.

Thus, with my duty humbly laid before you, I remain,

*Your lordship’s faithful servant,*  
*Edmund Vale*
