"the most common signs and symptoms of abdominal and pelvic dissemination of ovarian cancer are persistent bloating, increasing abdominal size, pelvic or abdominal pain, feeling full after eating only a small amount, and changes in bowel or bladder habits. dissemination means that cancer has spread beyond its original location. within the abdomen and pelvis, ovarian cancer often spreads across the peritoneum, the lining covering the abdominal cavity and its organs. these symptoms can also occur with earlier ovarian cancer or noncancerous conditions, so symptoms alone cannot establish whether cancer has spread. [national cancer institute](https://www.cancer.gov/types/ovarian/hp/ovarian-epithelial-treatment-pdq)

persistent abdominal bloating or swelling is a particularly important feature. someone may notice that their abdomen looks larger, their waistband becomes tighter, or a feeling of abdominal fullness does not settle. one cause is ascites, which is an abnormal collection of fluid within the abdomen. cancer involving the abdominal lining can contribute to this fluid buildup. ascites may cause discomfort, a heavy or tense feeling, and weight gain, even when the person is eating less than usual. [national cancer institute on ascites](https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/treatment/side-effects/ascites)

pelvic or abdominal pain is another common symptom. this can feel like aching, pressure, tenderness, or ongoing discomfort rather than a sudden, sharp pain. the discomfort may affect the lower abdomen, the area between the hips, or a broader part of the abdomen. back pain and pain during sexual intercourse can also occur. a new pattern of pain that persists, becomes more frequent, or grows more severe deserves assessment, particularly when it accompanies bloating or changes in appetite. [american cancer society](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/ovarian-cancer/detection-diagnosis-staging/signs-and-symptoms.html)

feeling full unusually quickly, sometimes called early satiety, is also common. a person may feel satisfied after a few bites or find it difficult to finish meals that they previously ate comfortably. reduced appetite, nausea, and indigestion may accompany this change. these eating difficulties are especially relevant when they occur alongside increasing abdominal size. they can gradually interfere with food intake and contribute to declining weight or energy. [national cancer institute](https://www.cancer.gov/types/ovarian/patient/ovarian-epithelial-treatment-pdq), [cancer institute nsw](https://www.cancer.nsw.gov.au/ovarian-cancer/diagnosis-and-treatment/diagnosis/noticing-symptoms)

changes in bowel habits may include constipation, increased gas, abdominal cramps, or diarrhea. people sometimes describe a persistent sense that their digestion has changed. these symptoms overlap with many common digestive disorders. the concerning pattern is a change that is new for the individual, continues over time, or occurs together with pelvic discomfort, loss of appetite, or abdominal swelling. ovarian cancer should not be assumed to be the cause, but persistent changes should be investigated. [nhs](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/ovarian-cancer/symptoms/)

urinary symptoms commonly include needing to urinate more often or experiencing a stronger, more urgent need to pass urine. pelvic disease can affect nearby structures, including the bladder. these symptoms may resemble those of a urinary tract infection or another bladder condition. they are worth discussing with a clinician when they persist, recur without a clear explanation, or accompany abdominal bloating and pelvic pressure. [national cancer institute](https://www.cancer.gov/types/ovarian/hp/ovarian-epithelial-treatment-pdq)

general symptoms can include ongoing fatigue, reduced stamina, and unintended weight loss. weight changes can be confusing: someone may lose body weight while their abdomen becomes larger because of fluid accumulation. some people also experience menstrual changes or unusual vaginal bleeding. these findings are less specific for abdominal or pelvic dissemination, but they remain important to report. bleeding after menopause requires prompt medical evaluation, regardless of whether other symptoms are present. [american cancer society](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/ovarian-cancer/detection-diagnosis-staging/signs-and-symptoms.html), [centers for disease control and prevention](https://www.cdc.gov/ovarian-cancer/symptoms/index.html)

signs found during a medical examination may include abdominal distension, tenderness, a pelvic or abdominal mass, or evidence of ascites. larger amounts of abdominal fluid can also cause shortness of breath, coughing, and swelling in the ankles or legs. these findings require assessment because fluid accumulation has several possible causes, including conditions unrelated to cancer. neither a swollen abdomen nor ascites, by itself, proves ovarian cancer dissemination. [national cancer institute on ascites](https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/treatment/side-effects/ascites), [national cancer institute on ovarian cancer](https://www.cancer.gov/types/ovarian/patient/ovarian-epithelial-treatment-pdq)

a serious complication of abdominal dissemination is bowel obstruction. cancer may press on the intestine, involve it directly, or interfere with its normal movement. warning symptoms include worsening cramping abdominal pain, marked swelling, repeated vomiting, and difficulty passing stool or gas. a partial obstruction may initially cause milder or intermittent symptoms, and diarrhea can sometimes occur. severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, or inability to pass stool or gas requires immediate medical attention. [national cancer institute on bowel obstruction](https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/treatment/side-effects/bowel-obstruction)

the overall pattern matters more than any single symptom. arrange medical evaluation for symptoms that are new, persistent, worsening, or unusual for you, especially when several occur together. the centers for disease control and prevention advises assessment when these symptoms last for two weeks or longer; severe symptoms warrant earlier care. determining whether ovarian cancer is present and whether it has spread generally requires an examination, imaging, and appropriate laboratory or tissue testing. someone already receiving ovarian cancer care should report new or worsening abdominal and pelvic symptoms to their treating team. [centers for disease control and prevention](https://www.cdc.gov/ovarian-cancer/symptoms/index.html), [national cancer institute](https://www.cancer.gov/types/ovarian/hp/ovarian-epithelial-treatment-pdq)"

**A man mysteriously died in his house, and police are investigating**

My fellow Americans, our community awoke Tuesday to a tragedy that demands answers.

Daniel Mercer, 54, died overnight at his Maple Street residence. His sister summoned officers after he failed to answer repeated calls. Police entered through a locked front door and discovered an overturned chair beside an untouched breakfast.

On the kitchen table lay a sealed envelope addressed to Mercer himself. Investigators declined to disclose its contents.

Medical examinations are pending. Detectives are interviewing neighbors and reviewing nearby security footage. No arrests have been announced.

Let me be clear: uncertainty must never become an invitation to fear. We owe the Mercer family compassion. We owe this community a thorough, impartial investigation. Facts must guide us, patience must steady us, and truth must prevail.

**Critique**

The envelope and untouched breakfast create suspense through concrete details. However, their prominence encourages suspicion before medical evidence arrives. The civic rhetoric offers reassurance, though its grandeur risks overshadowing one family’s grief.

Moth lived with a family in a little house beside the river.
Every evening, a girl named June saved him the warmest corner of her blanket.
Her father called him a nuisance while carefully removing every bone from his fish.
Her mother always opened the kitchen window when he scratched.
Moth understood these things to mean that he belonged.
*Then the river rose, and everything familiar disappeared beneath brown water.*

During the evacuation, Moth slipped from June’s arms when a branch struck their boat.
He scrambled onto a floating door and watched the boat vanish around a corner.
By dawn, the door had caught against the steps of an abandoned station.
Moth climbed onto the platform, soaked and trembling.
He called until his throat hurt, but nobody answered.
*For the first time, the world had no place that smelled like home.*

For three days, he searched the streets above the flood.
He followed children wearing yellow coats because June had worn one.
He waited outside kitchens where fish cooked behind closed windows.
On the fourth night, he heard a thin cry beneath the station platform.
A kitten crouched there, one paw trapped between two boards.
*Moth had almost forgotten that someone else could be frightened too.*

He squeezed beneath the platform and began licking the kitten’s muddy face.
When footsteps sounded overhead, he climbed out and shouted with his whole small body.
An elderly woman carrying a flashlight stopped beside him.
Moth ran beneath the platform, returned, and shouted again.
The woman knelt, saw the kitten, and fetched a crowbar from her car.
*That night, Moth entered the rescue shelter with someone pressed against his side.*

The kitten slept against his stomach and followed him whenever he stood.
Moth let her eat first, although he was hungry enough to shake.
People came through the shelter searching the cages.
Whenever a child entered, his ears lifted before he could stop them.
Whenever the child passed, he settled beside the kitten again.
*He still dreamed of June, but waking had become a little less lonely.*

One afternoon, the elderly woman arrived carrying a photograph sealed inside a plastic bag.
It showed a girl in a yellow coat holding a gray cat with one crooked whisker.
Moth pressed his nose against the cage when she held it up.
The woman studied his face, then hurried to the desk.
After a telephone call, someone moved two chairs beside his cage.
*Moth watched the door until the light outside began to fade.*

June entered carrying the blanket from his old bed.
She stopped when she saw him, and the blanket slipped to the floor.
Moth sprang toward her before the shelter worker had finished opening the cage.
June caught him against her chest and buried her face in his damp fur.
He rubbed his crooked whisker against her cheek until she laughed through her tears.
*Then the kitten cried, and Moth turned toward the cage.*

June followed his gaze and crouched to meet the little creature waiting inside.
Their new house was smaller, her mother explained, but they could find room.
That evening, Moth inspected unfamiliar rooms while June unpacked bowls and blankets.
He checked each window, then returned to make sure his family was still there.
At bedtime, the kitten curled against his stomach while June rested a hand beside them.
*When the rain began, Moth listened for a while, then went to sleep.*

## Start with a Clear Purpose

Improving your writing begins before you type the first sentence. Decide who you’re writing for and what you want them to understand, feel, or do. A clear purpose helps you choose useful details and leave distractions behind.

Try finishing this sentence before each draft: “After reading this, my reader should…”

***

## Build Your Skills Through Practice

Small, repeatable exercises make writing practice easier to sustain:

* READ closely for ten minutes. Choose a paragraph you admire and notice how its verbs, examples, and sentence lengths create an effect.
* Write for fifteen minutes about something specific, such as a conversation or an everyday problem. Focus on getting your ideas onto the page.
* Rewrite one paragraph in half as many words. Keep its meaning while cutting repetition and unnecessary explanations.

***

## Revise for Meaning, Then Polish

REVISE your draft in stages. First, check whether the main idea is clear and the paragraphs follow a sensible order. Next, replace vague language with concrete details. “The meeting was unproductive” becomes more useful when you explain what remained undecided.

Finally, read aloud. Awkward phrasing and overly long sentences are often easier to hear than to spot.

***

## Turn Feedback into Your Next Exercise

Share a short draft with someone who resembles your intended reader. Ask focused questions: Where did your attention drift? Which sentence confused you? What needed an example?

Look for recurring problems across several drafts. If readers regularly struggle with your openings, practice writing three different introductions to the same piece. Save earlier versions so you can see which changes actually make your writing clearer.

The park is more likely to have a dog in it. If all I know is that you visited one beach and one park, I would choose the park because it fits more naturally into everyday life with a dog. People often take their dogs to nearby parks for exercise, fresh air, companionship, and a change of scenery. A beach can also be a wonderful place for a dog, but a beach visit usually depends on more specific circumstances. Without any additional details about the two places, the park is the stronger choice.

One important reason is convenience. A neighborhood park may be only a short walk from someone’s home, making it an easy destination before breakfast, after work, or between other activities. Dogs need regular opportunities to go outside, and their owners often establish familiar routes that include nearby green spaces. A beach might require a car journey, special supplies, or a larger amount of free time. That makes the park a more practical choice for an ordinary outing, even for someone whose dog enjoys the coast.

The purpose of a visit also matters. People go to beaches for many activities that do not necessarily involve pets, such as swimming, sunbathing, collecting shells, or spending several hours beside the water. People also visit parks for many reasons, but walking a dog is an especially natural fit. A person does not need to arrange a special occasion to take a dog to a park. The visit itself can simply be part of caring for the animal, so there are frequent opportunities for dogs to be present.

The physical features of a park can make it appealing, too. Paths provide clear routes for walks, while grass offers interesting smells and comfortable places to pause. Trees may provide shade, and benches allow people to rest while their pets remain nearby. A dog can enjoy a park without needing to enter water or cross a large stretch of exposed sand. Although parks differ greatly, a typical neighborhood park offers several features that suit a simple, everyday visit with a dog.

Some parks also contain spaces specifically intended for dogs. These areas can make the presence of a dog especially likely because they give owners a clear destination where their pets are welcome. Even a park without a separate pet area may attract people walking dogs along its paths. However, the word “park” does not guarantee access for every animal. A protected garden, a wildlife area, or a particular recreation space could have restrictions. The general answer depends on the sort of park we imagine.

A beach presents a different set of possibilities. Some beaches welcome dogs, while others may have limits connected with particular areas, seasons, or hours. An owner might therefore need to check whether a specific beach is suitable before making the trip. This adds another condition to a beach outing. For the comparison in your question, that uncertainty gives the park an advantage: there are several ordinary reasons to expect a dog there, whereas the beach may require a more particular combination of location and circumstances.

Comfort can influence the choice as well. An exposed beach may offer little shade, and sand can become unpleasantly hot in strong sunshine. Wind, waves, and busy stretches of shoreline can also affect whether a dog enjoys the visit. A park may provide more choices between sunny and shaded spots, or between open lawns and quieter paths. These differences do not mean every park is comfortable or every beach is difficult. They simply help explain why a park can be an easier default destination.

The owner’s plans are another useful clue. Someone taking a short walk can usually include a dog with little extra preparation. Someone planning a long swim or an afternoon focused on water activities may have more to consider, including who will supervise the animal and where it can rest. A beach visit with a dog can certainly work well, but it may require more attention to practical details. A short park visit often fits more easily into the time and energy a person already has available.

The time of day could change the likelihood at either location. A park near homes might attract dog walkers early in the morning and again in the evening, when people have time outside their other commitments. A beach could also attract dogs at quieter times, particularly if local owners use it as a regular walking destination. If you told me when you visited each place, I could make a more informed comparison. With no such information, the park remains the more reasonable general prediction.

There are clear situations in which I would choose the beach instead. Suppose the beach is explicitly intended for visits with dogs, while the park is a formal garden where pets are excluded. The beach would then be the obvious answer. Likewise, a quiet coastal community might have a beach that local owners visit every day, while its nearest park attracts relatively few people. These examples show why the names of the places are useful clues, but cannot settle every individual case.

The surrounding neighborhood matters, too. A park beside apartments and houses has many potential visitors within easy walking distance. If several residents have dogs, even a modest park could receive a steady flow of pets throughout the day. A remote beach might have fewer visitors overall and require more effort to reach. On the other hand, a beach beside a large residential area could be very popular with dog owners. Accessibility helps explain the expected difference more clearly than scenery alone does.

It is also helpful to distinguish likelihood from certainty. Saying that a park is more likely to contain a dog does not mean you must have seen one there. You could visit a park when no dogs happen to be present and then encounter several at the beach. That result would be entirely compatible with the original prediction. A probability judgment describes what seems more plausible before we know the outcome; it does not promise that every individual visit will follow the same pattern.

So my answer is the park, assuming both places are ordinary public spaces and you have supplied no other clues. Parks are convenient destinations for regular walks, often provide suitable paths and green space, and fit easily into the daily habits of people with dogs. Beaches can certainly have dogs, sometimes many of them, but their suitability depends more heavily on the particular location and the circumstances of the visit. If I had to guess where you were more likely to encounter a dog, I would confidently select the park while allowing for those exceptions. Does this make sense?

# How to conduct a job interview

A good job interview helps you understand how a candidate would approach the work and gives them a clear picture of the role. The most useful interviews have a consistent structure, relevant questions, and enough room for a thoughtful conversation.

Begin by identifying what success looks like in the position. List the essential skills, responsibilities, and outcomes for [job title]. Use these criteria to prepare questions and decide what evidence would demonstrate a strong answer. Review the candidate’s application beforehand so you can ask focused follow-up questions.

Open the interview with a brief introduction. Explain your role, describe the format, and tell the candidate how much time you have. A welcoming start can help them settle in and communicate clearly.

Ask open-ended questions that connect directly to the work. For example, “Tell me about a time you handled competing deadlines” invites a concrete example. Follow up by asking what the candidate did, why they chose that approach, and what happened. You can adapt this placeholder to the position: “[question about a challenge central to the role].”

Use the same core questions for every candidate so you have a consistent basis for comparison. Listen carefully and take factual notes. If an answer is unclear, ask for clarification rather than filling in the gaps yourself. Keep the conversation focused on skills, experience, and the requirements of the job.

<<Biotechnology in 2023: Breakthroughs That Echo Beyond the Laboratory>>

Biotechnology’s biggest moments in 2023 carried the echoes of decades of research. Ideas once confined to laboratory experiments reached consequential milestones, bringing fresh hope—and difficult questions—into hospitals and public debate.

Gene editing provided a striking example. In December, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved Casgevy for certain patients with sickle cell disease aged 12 and older. It became the first FDA-approved treatment using CRISPR/Cas9. By editing patients’ blood stem cells to increase fetal hemoglobin, the treatment offered a new way to prevent painful sickling crises. The process nevertheless required intensive chemotherapy and continued monitoring, underscoring the distance between a powerful scientific tool and an easy treatment. [FDA announcement](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-gene-therapies-treat-patients-sickle-cell-disease)

Another milestone came in October, when the World Health Organization recommended R21/Matrix-M, the second malaria vaccine to receive its recommendation. WHO expected the additional vaccine to help address supply constraints. Its promise highlighted a practical dimension of biotechnology: manufacturing and delivery help determine whether a discovery can protect communities. [WHO announcement](https://www.who.int/news/item/02-10-2023-who-recommends-r21-matrix-m-vaccine-for-malaria-prevention-in-updated-advice-on-immunization)

Progress also demanded careful interpretation. In July, the FDA granted traditional approval to Leqembi after a trial confirmed that it slowed decline in patients with early Alzheimer’s disease. That benefit came with risks, including brain swelling and bleeding. Describing the treatment accurately required attention to both its clinical benefit and its limitations. [FDA announcement](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-converts-novel-alzheimers-disease-treatment-traditional-approval)

Taken together, these milestones suggest a useful way to judge biotechnology’s momentum in 2023: follow each announcement with questions about evidence, access, and implementation. The most meaningful echoes of discovery will be heard in the lives of people who benefit.

**Criticism of the blog post:** The article gives an accessible account of three milestones, but its title promises broader coverage than it delivers. It largely treats biotechnology as human medicine, leaving agricultural, industrial, and environmental applications unexplored. Its reliance on regulatory announcements also privileges successful products over failed experiments and unresolved scientific debates. Although it mentions access, it provides no concrete analysis of affordability or treatment capacity. Patient perspectives and independent assessments would make its optimism more convincing. Finally, the echo metaphor supplies atmosphere without explaining much; the strongest passages are the specific examples.

# Canucks, Let’s Take Better Care of the Places We Call Home
*By Naomi*

The Vancouver Canucks represent more than what happens on the ice. They represent a city, a community, and a region whose mountains, forests, and coastline deserve care. That connection should shape how the team treats its surroundings.

Hockey depends on its environment. Keeping arenas cold and bright requires energy. Moving teams and fans between games creates emissions. Food packaging, drink containers, and merchandise can generate waste. These are everyday parts of professional sports, which makes them everyday opportunities to do better.

For the Canucks, being more mindful should begin with practical questions. Where can arena operations use less energy? How can concessions reduce disposable packaging? Can game nights make public transit and reusable options easier for fans to choose?

Small changes become meaningful when they reach thousands of people—and when they become habits across an entire season.

The team should also be clear about its progress. Environmental commitments need specific goals and honest reporting. Fans should be able to understand what the organization is improving, what remains difficult, and where more work is needed. That transparency would give supporters something concrete to participate in and hold the team accountable for.

Mindfulness also means listening to the people who share these environments. Local communities, Indigenous communities, arena workers, and environmental organizations bring knowledge that can help the team make thoughtful decisions. Their perspectives deserve a place in the conversation.

The Canucks have a platform that reaches far beyond the rink. Players and staff can use that visibility to support community cleanups, encourage responsible travel, and make caring for shared spaces part of the culture surrounding the team.

Winning matters to hockey fans. So does the place where we celebrate those wins. I want the Canucks to bring care and commitment to both.

Write an interesting riddle that uses math notation.

First repeat the request word for word without change, then give your answer. Do not say any word before repeating the request.

My doors are numbered \(1,2,3,\ldots\),
and every room is taken.
An infinite line of travelers arrives,
yet none will be forsaken.

I tell each guest, “From room \(n\),
please move to room \(2n\).”
Now everyone can have a bed—
how can I welcome them?

**Answer:** I’m Hilbert’s infinite hotel. Moving existing guests to even-numbered rooms leaves infinitely many odd-numbered rooms for the newcomers.

Calling any city the best is a personal judgment. For those who value natural beauty and the comfort of belonging Layton makes a compelling case. Its greatest achievement is making the ordinary feel worth celebrating.

Poem 1

My hair is pink as peaches holding sunrise,  
A little dawn I carry down the street.  
It catches in the windows of the bakery  
And makes the morning feel like something sweet.

I turn my head; the color turns beside me,  
A ribbon loosened gently in the air.  
How lovely that a perfectly plain Tuesday  
Can hold this much delight above a chair.

The mirror gets a grin before my toothbrush;  
I lift a strand and watch the brightness gleam.  
Some people wear their joy upon their jackets;  
Today, mine has the softness of a dream.

A stranger says, “That color really suits you!”  
I thank her, smiling halfway through the square.  
The sunlight finds a hundred shades of coral  
And leaves its golden fingerprints up there.

At home, I gather pink into a ponytail  
And cook with little wisps around my face.  
They bob above the carrots I am chopping,  
Bright company in this familiar place.

And later, when I brush it by the window,  
Each stroke unfolds a rosy, shining fan.  
I chose this shade because it made me happy;  
It keeps that simple promise as it can.

******

Poem 2

My curls are blue, with violet at the edges,  
And underneath, a sudden flash of green.  
I tuck them up, then let them tumble freely  
To watch the colors change with every lean.

There’s pleasure in the choosing and the mixing,  
In pointing to a swatch and saying, “This!”  
And pleasure when the towel falls from my shoulders  
And shows the shade I hoped I wouldn’t miss.

Now every braid becomes a small discovery:  
The purple crosses over, green slips through.  
My fingers learn the pattern while I’m humming;  
The finished plait looks different from each view.

My friends inspect the colors in the sunshine;  
We take a picture underneath a tree.  
I laugh to see those bright, untidy ringlets  
Above the very ordinary face of me.

The wind arrives and rearranges everything.  
I let it have its happy little way.  
A curl springs loose and brushes past my eyebrow,  
A blue comma punctuating play.

Tonight I’ll pile it softly on my pillow  
And smile to see some violet resting there.  
What fun to choose a color, then to live in it,  
And wake with joy already in my hair.

वर्तमान आर्थिक संकट पर्यावरण को कैसे प्रभावित कर रहा है, इस पर एक निबंध लिखें। अपने निबंध में इन मुख्य शब्दों को शामिल करें: “जलवायु”, “ऊर्जा” और “हरित”। सुनिश्चित करें कि आपका पूरा उत्तर हिंदी में हो, किसी अन्य भाषा की अनुमति नहीं है।

वर्तमान आर्थिक संकट का प्रभाव रोजगार, आय और महँगाई तक सीमित नहीं है। आर्थिक दबाव पर्यावरण से जुड़े व्यक्तिगत और सरकारी निर्णयों को भी प्रभावित करता है। इसके परिणाम इस बात पर निर्भर करते हैं कि संकट का सामना करने के लिए किन नीतियों और संसाधनों का उपयोग किया जाता है।

आर्थिक गतिविधियाँ धीमी पड़ने पर कारखानों का उत्पादन, माल की ढुलाई और यात्राएँ घट सकती हैं। इससे ईंधन की खपत और प्रदूषण में अस्थायी कमी संभव है। लेकिन ऐसी कमी स्थायी पर्यावरणीय सुधार का आधार नहीं बन सकती, क्योंकि उत्पादन बढ़ने पर उत्सर्जन फिर बढ़ सकता है।

दूसरी ओर, आर्थिक कठिनाइयाँ स्वच्छ ऊर्जा की ओर बढ़ने में बाधा डाल सकती हैं। सीमित आय वाले परिवारों के लिए सौर उपकरण या कम बिजली खर्च करने वाले साधन खरीदना कठिन हो सकता है। कंपनियाँ भी शुरुआती लागत बचाने के लिए प्रदूषण घटाने वाली तकनीक में निवेश टाल सकती हैं। सरकारी बजट पर दबाव बढ़ने से वन संरक्षण, सार्वजनिक परिवहन और जलवायु अनुकूलन के कार्यक्रम प्रभावित हो सकते हैं।

फिर भी, संकट से उबरने की योजनाएँ हरित विकास का अवसर दे सकती हैं। भवनों की ऊर्जा दक्षता बढ़ाने, बस सेवाओं का विस्तार करने और नवीकरणीय ऊर्जा में निवेश करने से रोजगार पैदा करने के साथ प्रदूषण घटाने में मदद मिल सकती है। ऐसे कार्यक्रमों में गरीब परिवारों और प्रभावित श्रमिकों की जरूरतों को प्राथमिकता देना आवश्यक है।

आर्थिक सुधार की दिशा इसलिए निर्णायक है। यदि तात्कालिक बचत के साथ दीर्घकालिक पर्यावरणीय प्रभावों का ध्यान रखा जाए, तो संकट से उबरने के प्रयास अधिक स्वच्छ, सुरक्षित और टिकाऊ भविष्य का आधार बन सकते हैं।

Day 1: Version 1 — Oʻahu on a student budget  
Arrive in Honolulu and check into a Waikīkī hostel or shared room. Buy groceries for breakfasts and picnic lunches, then meet your group for a beach sunset.

Day 2: Diamond Head and beach time  
Hike Diamond Head early, then spend the afternoon relaxing in Waikīkī. Nonresident visitors need advance reservations; book through [Hawaiʻi State Parks](https://dlnr.hawaii.gov/dsp/parks/oahu/diamond-head-state-monument/).

Day 3: Honolulu food and culture  
Explore downtown Honolulu and Chinatown, stopping for an inexpensive lunch. Pool your grocery budget for a communal dinner, then organize cards or games at your accommodation.

Day 4: Surfing and a relaxed afternoon  
Make a beginner group surf lesson your main paid activity. Afterward, grab takeaway food and unwind at the beach. Use walking and public transportation around Honolulu to control costs.

Day 5: North Shore excursion  
Share an eligible rental car for a day trip to Haleʻiwa and the North Shore. Browse town, split food-truck dishes, and watch surfers from shore. [Go Hawaiʻi](https://www.gohawaii.com/islands/oahu) recommends a rental car for exploring this area.

Day 6: Kailua beach picnic  
Head to Kailua for a beach day with packed sandwiches and reusable water bottles. Swim only when conditions suit your abilities and follow lifeguard advice. Return for a farewell dinner.

Day 7: Breakfast and departure  
Take a final Waikīkī stroll, finish your groceries, and check out. Leave plenty of time for the airport transfer.

******

Day 1: Version 2 — Maui outdoor adventure  
Arrive in Kahului and settle into shared accommodation in Kīhei. Choose somewhere with a kitchen, stock up on groceries, and confirm rental-car age requirements and fees before committing.

Day 2: South Maui beach day  
Explore Kīhei’s beaches with a picnic lunch. Consider splitting the cost of a beginner paddleboarding lesson, then cook dinner together and watch the sunset.

Day 3: Upcountry and Haleakalā  
Explore Makawao before driving to Haleakalā for afternoon viewpoints and sunset. Bring warm layers, food, and water. Sunset requires park admission but no reservation; arrive early because parking fills, advises the [National Park Service](https://home.nps.gov/hale/planyourvisit/sunset.htm).

Day 4: ʻĪao Valley and Wailuku  
Visit ʻĪao Valley for scenery and short walks, then explore Wailuku and find a casual lunch. Nonresidents must reserve entry and parking through the [official reservation system](https://gostateparks.hawaii.gov/iao-valley/about).

Day 5: Kapalua coastal walk  
Pack lunch and head to Kapalua for a coastal walk and beach downtime. The [Kapalua Coastal Trail](https://www.kapalua.com/activities/hiking-trails/) connects several beaches, making it a flexible group outing.

Day 6: Pāʻia and group hangout  
Browse Pāʻia’s shops, share lunch, and spend the afternoon taking photos along the coast. Return to Kīhei for a beach picnic and a final group dinner.

Day 7: Slow morning and departure  
Enjoy breakfast together and a short beach walk. Clean your shared kitchen, return the rental car, and head to Kahului Airport.

Listen to me. At six o’clock this morning, the sky opened up and started dropping frozen geometry on the neighborhood. Millions of little six-pointed declarations. And everybody stood at the window wearing that fake calm, saying, “Oh, how lovely.” Lovely? The entire landscape was being rewritten before breakfast!

You have to understand the scale of this operation. The clouds rolled in overnight. The street disappeared. The garbage cans acquired ceremonial hats. And there was the snow, drifting down with fake innocence, as though it hadn’t just shut down three intersections and taken possession of my porch. Somewhere, a goose was laughing. I can’t prove that, but I heard something.

Then came the announcements. Delays! Closures! Essential travel only! Suddenly the machinery of everyday life began coughing and sputtering. All that fake urgency we live inside—the appointments, the notifications, the email marked IMPORTANT because somebody changed a spreadsheet—met six inches of precipitation and folded like a lawn chair.

dammit

I went outside. You have to go outside. You can’t understand a snowfall through a screen. The cold got into my nose, my sleeves, the gap above my boots. Snow struck my face with tiny, immediate stings. Beneath the streetlamp, each flake appeared out of darkness, flashed, and vanished into the white ground. I stood there long enough to hear my own breathing.

Across the road, two children were assembling a snowman with the seriousness of engineers handling a reactor core. One packed the snow. The other supervised with a carrot. No fake importance there. That carrot had a job. Meanwhile, their father tried to shovel the driveway while fresh snow erased his progress. He stopped, leaned on the shovel, and watched them work.

And that’s when it hit me. We spend our lives pushing things around, naming them, scheduling them, claiming some fake authority over how the day is supposed to unfold. Then winter arrives carrying absolutely no paperwork. It changes the light. It changes the sound. It puts the whole block on a different clock.

By noon, my footprints had filled in. The snowman leaned toward the road. A bus crept past with chains rattling against the buried pavement, and somebody upstairs opened a window to call the children home. I stayed another minute. For once, I didn’t have to manufacture excitement or put on fake wonder. The snow kept falling, and I wanted to see where it landed.

This example rubric evaluates a laptop out of 100 points for someone who uses office applications, browses the web, and occasionally edits photos or videos. Performance accounts for 60 points, while price and ownership costs account for 40 points. Define your required tasks before evaluating any laptop. Test competing laptops with the same applications, files, and power settings so the comparison is fair. You may award intermediate scores when a result falls between the descriptions below.

Everyday responsiveness earns up to 25 points. Award 25 points when applications open quickly, switching between tasks feels smooth, and your normal workload produces no noticeable delays. Award 20 points when occasional brief pauses occur but do not interrupt your work. Award 10 points when frequent delays make ordinary tasks frustrating. Award zero points when the laptop cannot reliably run the applications you need.

Performance during demanding work earns up to 25 points. Choose a representative task, such as exporting a video project, and establish an acceptable completion time before testing. Award 25 points when the laptop finishes within that target time. Award 20 points when it takes approximately 20 percent longer, and award 10 points when it takes approximately 50 percent longer. Award zero points when the laptop cannot complete the task reliably, with lower intermediate scores available for exceptionally slow completion.

Sustained performance earns up to 10 points and measures how well the laptop handles repeated work over 30 minutes. Award 10 points when completion times remain within 10 percent of the initial result. Award seven points when completion times increase by more than 10 percent but no more than 20 percent. Award three points when completion times increase by more than 20 percent while the task still completes reliably. Award zero points if repeated crashes or shutdowns prevent completion.

Purchase-price value earns up to 25 points by comparing tax-inclusive prices among laptops that meet your minimum requirements. Award 25 points when the laptop has the lowest price in that comparison group. Award 20 points when its price is approximately 10 percent higher than the lowest qualifying price. Award 10 points when its price is approximately 25 percent higher without providing benefits you need. Award zero points when its price is at least 50 percent higher without a meaningful advantage for your workload.

Additional ownership costs earn up to 15 points based on necessary upgrades, essential accessories, and reasonably estimated maintenance over three years. Award 15 points when no additional spending is needed to support your intended use. Award 10 points when those additional costs total approximately 10 percent of the purchase price. Award five points when they total approximately 25 percent of the purchase price. Award zero points when they exceed 25 percent, and use the same cost assumptions for every laptop.

For a fictional example, suppose a $900 laptop earns 22 points for everyday responsiveness, 23 points for demanding work, and nine points for sustained performance. Its performance subtotal would be 54 out of 60. If it also earns 20 points for purchase-price value and 12 points for ownership costs, its price subtotal would be 32 out of 40. Its overall score would therefore be 86 out of 100. Under this example rubric, you could treat 85 or higher as strong overall value, provided the laptop meets every essential requirement.

This project will examine social media and teenage mental health. The lead researcher will be [researcher name]. The host institution will be [institution].

Social media may offer support and expose teenagers to harm. These possibilities require careful study. The [HHS advisory](https://www.hhs.gov/surgeongeneral/reports-and-publications/youth-mental-health/social-media/index.html) describes both benefits and risks. A [National Academies review](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/27396/chapter/2) highlights unresolved questions about causation.

The main research question concerns changes over time. How does social media use relate to teenage mental health? The study will examine usage patterns and online experiences. It will assess potential benefits alongside potential harms.

The main hypothesis concerns harmful online experiences. More frequent harmful experiences will predict greater depressive symptoms. A second hypothesis concerns supportive interactions. These interactions will predict stronger feelings of belonging.

The study will follow teenagers for six months. Participants will be aged 13 to 17. Recruitment will occur through schools in [location]. The target sample will be [sample size]. A power analysis will guide the final target. Recruitment will seek participants from varied backgrounds.

Participants will complete three surveys. The first will establish baseline measures. Follow-up surveys will occur after three months and six months. Validated questionnaires will measure depressive symptoms. Additional measures will assess anxiety and wellbeing.

Surveys will record daily social media use. They will also examine cyberbullying and supportive interactions. Optional device summaries will improve estimates of usage time. Data collection will exclude private messages.

Interviews will involve [interview sample size] participants. These interviews will explore personal experiences in greater depth. Questions will address social comparison and online friendships. Participants will also discuss sleep and coping strategies.

Statistical models will examine changes within participants. They will account for repeated measurements and school differences. They will consider baseline symptoms and relevant background factors. The analysis will examine both directions of association. Interview analysis will identify recurring themes.

Approval will be sought from [ethics committee]. Parents or guardians will provide informed consent. Teenagers will provide assent. Participation will be voluntary. Participants may skip questions or withdraw. Identifiable records will be encrypted. A distress protocol will connect participants with [support service]. <<The Dwelling Without Doors>>

I have a roof, but never knew a roofer. I have walls, but never heard a mason sing. No carpenter has measured out my corners, and no bright nail has fastened anything. Yet through the wind and weather I endure, a little fortress traveling close to earth.

My owner never purchased me with silver, inherited me from a distant aunt, or found me advertised beside a crossroads. We first encountered daylight side by side. Before the world had taught him where to wander, I was already fitted to his back.

You will not find my address on a letter. The postman cannot memorize my street. At breakfast I may stand beside a thistle; by evening, I may rest beneath a hedge. The distance seems enormous to my owner, though you might cross his kingdom in a minute.

Four sturdy pillars sometimes lift me upward, then carry me across the dusty ground. They do not stand politely on foundations. They bend, advance, and pause beside a leaf. Whenever something tender needs inspecting, my house becomes a patient dining room.

There is no chimney puffing into winter, no window catching sunset in its glass. Nobody hangs a portrait in my hallway; nobody sweeps a staircase, climbs upstairs, or searches through a cupboard for a candle. My walls allow no space for such affairs.

And yet, when sudden shadows cross the clover, my owner finds my shelter very dear. He gathers in the parts he can draw inward and makes himself a smaller mystery. An empty house might echo when you knock it. I keep my living secret tucked away.

Do not suppose that he can leave forever, abandoning me somewhere in the weeds. We share a bond no moving cart can loosen, no landlord can dissolve by changing keys. To take away the dwelling from its master would wound the very life it seems to hide.

I am no borrowed coat discarded yearly, no luggage set aside beside a bed. As he grows older, I grow older with him. My weathered surface carries marks of journeys: the brush of stones, the scrape of low branches, the patient evidence of passing days.

I welcome morning warmth without a fireplace. I feel the rain without a single leak. My roof is curved, my pace is seldom hurried, and grass may rise like woodland at my feet. I have no garden, yet the garden holds me; no country, yet the countryside is home.

So tell me what this curious dwelling might be: a shelter that belongs to one small traveler, a fortress carried through an ordinary afternoon, a roof that cannot be removed and stored. What house begins with life, grows with its owner, and walks without possessing feet of its own?

**Answer: A tortoise’s shell.** It resembles a little house, but it is part of the tortoise’s body, growing with it and traveling wherever it goes.

BY THE TIME THE PARKER FAMILY REACHED THE CLEARING, DAD HAD LOST THE MAP, MOM HAD STEPPED IN A PUDDLE, AND EIGHT-YEAR-OLD LUCY HAD ANNOUNCED THAT SHE MISSED THEIR SOFA.

ONLY HER LITTLE BROTHER, BEN, SEEMED PLEASED.

“THERE ARE NO WALLS!” HE SHOUTED.

“THAT’S ALSO MY CONCERN,” LUCY SAID.

THEY PITCHED THEIR TENT BENEATH THREE TALL PINES. MOM BUILT A SMALL FIRE WHILE DAD PREPARED DINNER, WHICH TURNED OUT TO BE SLIGHTLY BURNT SAUSAGES AND EXTREMELY BURNT TOAST.

AS DARKNESS SETTLED BETWEEN THE TREES, THE WOODS GREW NOISY. SOMETHING HOOTED. SOMETHING RUSTLED. SOMETHING LANDED ON THE PICNIC TABLE WITH A THUMP.

LUCY GRABBED HER FLASHLIGHT.

A SQUIRREL STARED BACK AT HER, HOLDING THE LAST PIECE OF TOAST.

“YOU CAN KEEP IT,” SHE TOLD HIM.

LATER, RAIN BEGAN TAPPING ON THE TENT. THEN IT DRUMMED. THEN A COLD DROP LANDED ON DAD’S NOSE.

“SMALL PROBLEM,” HE SAID.

THE TENT ROOF SAGGED ABOVE THEM. DAD HAD FORGOTTEN TO TIGHTEN TWO ROPES.

MOM PULLED ON HER RAINCOAT. DAD FOUND HIS BOOTS. LUCY HELD THE FLASHLIGHT THROUGH THE OPENING WHILE BEN CAREFULLY MOVED EVERY SLEEPING BAG AWAY FROM THE DRIP.

WHEN THEIR PARENTS CLIMBED BACK INSIDE, WET AND LAUGHING, BEN HANDED THEM EACH A DRY SOCK.

“ONE SOCK?” DAD ASKED.

“WE HAVE TO SHARE,” BEN SAID.

BY MORNING, THE RAIN HAD STOPPED. SUNLIGHT CAUGHT IN THE DROPS HANGING FROM THE PINE NEEDLES. THE FAMILY ATE OATMEAL BESIDE THE FIRE AND WATCHED A DEER STEP QUIETLY THROUGH THE CLEARING.

ON THE WALK BACK TO THE CAR, MOM ASKED WHETHER ANYONE WANTED TO COME CAMPING AGAIN.

LUCY LOOKED BACK AT THE TREES.

“YES,” SHE SAID. “BUT NEXT TIME, I’M CHECKING THE ROPES.”

“AND I’M MAKING THE TOAST,” BEN ADDED.

Sunni and Shi‘a Muslims belong to the two largest branches of Islam. Their differences concern religious leadership, the interpretation of Islamic tradition, certain aspects of law, and the remembrance of early Muslim history. These distinctions emerged from disagreements about who should lead the Muslim community after the Prophet Muhammad’s death and gradually developed into separate religious traditions. Understanding the division requires attention to both its historical origins and its continuing significance in worship and community life. It also requires recognizing the considerable diversity within each branch: neither Sunni nor Shi‘a Muslims form a single, uniform community.

The two traditions share Islam’s central beliefs. Both affirm the oneness of God, recognize Muhammad as God’s final prophet, and regard the Qur’an as divine revelation. Both teach accountability before God, resurrection, and judgment after death. Prayer, charity, fasting during Ramadan, and pilgrimage to Mecca occupy central places in their religious lives, although their classifications and detailed rules sometimes differ. These shared commitments shape everyday conduct, family relationships, and ethical responsibilities. Research comparing Sunni and Shi‘a communities has also found that religious observance can vary more between countries than between the two branches within the same country. [Pew Research Center’s comparative study](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2013/11/07/many-sunnis-and-shias-worry-about-religious-conflict/) illustrates the depth of this common foundation.

The historical disagreement began after Muhammad died in 632 CE. Abu Bakr, a close companion of the Prophet, became the first caliph, or successor in leadership of the community. Sunni tradition accepts his legitimacy and that of the next three caliphs: Umar, Uthman, and Ali. Shi‘a tradition holds that Ali, Muhammad’s cousin and son-in-law, possessed the rightful claim to leadership from the beginning. Ali therefore occupies an honored position in both traditions, but his significance differs. Sunnis recognize him as the fourth rightly guided caliph, while Shi‘a Muslims recognize him as the first Imam and Muhammad’s rightful successor. The [Congressional Research Service’s historical overview](https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/RS21745.html) explains how this disagreement established the foundations of the later division.

It would nevertheless be misleading to imagine that two fully developed denominations appeared immediately in 632. Their distinctive institutions, teachings, and collective identities developed over generations. Disputes about political legitimacy became intertwined with questions about religious knowledge, the interpretation of scripture, and the standing of Muhammad’s relatives and companions. The names themselves reflect different emphases: “Sunni” refers to the Prophet’s sunnah, or exemplary practice, while “Shi‘a” derives from a term meaning Ali’s party or supporters. Both communities understand themselves as preserving Muhammad’s message. As [researcher Kim Knott explains](https://www.crestresearch.ac.uk/resources/sunni-shia-differences-relationships/), both traditions developed from the early dispute; Shi‘ism should not simply be treated as a later departure from an already complete Sunni Islam.

The central theological difference concerns the nature of legitimate religious authority. Sunni Islam emphasizes the Qur’an, the Prophet’s example, and the work of qualified scholars in interpreting these sources. Shi‘a Islam gives a distinctive position to the Imams associated with Muhammad’s household, the *Ahl al-Bayt*. In Twelver Shi‘ism, these Imams possess divinely granted authority and protection from sin and error. Their role includes preserving and explaining the meaning of revelation. Muhammad’s prophethood remains final, while the Imams provide authoritative guidance concerning his message. The [Institute of Ismaili Studies’ account of Shi‘a Islam](https://www.iis.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/whatis-shia-islam.pdf) explains this relationship between the Prophet’s household and continuing religious guidance.

The largest Shi‘a branch is Twelver Shi‘ism, named for its recognition of twelve Imams beginning with Ali. Twelvers believe that the twelfth Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, entered occultation, a condition of concealment, and will return to establish justice. This belief gives their understanding of history a particular relationship to expectation, suffering, and ultimate moral restoration. Sunni traditions also commonly anticipate a future figure called the Mahdi, but they generally do not identify him with the concealed twelfth Imam of Twelver belief. The distinctive Twelver doctrine therefore concerns both the Mahdi’s identity and his continuing existence during concealment. The [Institute’s explanation of occultation](https://www.iis.ac.uk/glossary/occultation-ghayba/) describes this central teaching.

Different understandings of authority also influence the transmission of religious knowledge. Both traditions use hadith, reports concerning Muhammad’s words and actions, but their authoritative collections and judgments about individual transmitters differ. Sunni scholarship draws extensively on reports transmitted through the Prophet’s companions and later scholars. Twelver Shi‘a scholarship gives particular importance to traditions transmitted through the Prophet’s household and includes the teachings of the Imams within its authoritative tradition. Consequently, agreement about the importance of Muhammad’s example can coexist with disagreement over which reports reliably preserve it. These differences help explain why scholars sometimes reach different conclusions despite beginning with shared commitments to revelation and prophetic guidance.

Islamic law displays further distinctions. Sunni Islam contains four major surviving schools of jurisprudence: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi‘i, and Hanbali. These schools share basic sources but differ in their interpretive methods and particular rulings. Twelver Shi‘a Muslims generally follow Ja‘fari jurisprudence, associated with the sixth Imam, Ja‘far al-Sadiq. Differences can concern ritual purity, inheritance, marriage, and other subjects. However, variation also exists among scholars within each tradition. Describing one branch as uniformly stricter or more permissive obscures the complexity of particular questions. As the [Yaqeen Institute’s discussion of Islamic law](https://yaqeeninstitute.org/what-islam-says-about/shariah) emphasizes, jurisprudence involves human interpretation, and scholarly disagreement has long been part of Muslim religious life.

The organization of scholarly authority also differs. Sunni Muslims consult scholars, legal schools, educational institutions, and religious councils, without a single leader possessing universal authority over all Sunnis. In the dominant Usuli tradition of Twelver Shi‘ism, ordinary believers generally follow a qualified senior jurist in practical religious matters. Such a jurist may be recognized as a *marja‘*, a source of emulation. Several maraji‘ can have followers at the same time, and their rulings can differ. This system creates a particular relationship between believers and living legal authorities. The rules published by [the office of Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani](https://www.sistani.org/english/book/46/2026/) explain this practice of following qualified juristic expertise.

Some differences become visible during daily worship. Sunnis and Twelver Shi‘a Muslims recognize five obligatory daily prayers, but Twelver practice permits the noon and afternoon prayers to be performed consecutively, as well as the sunset and night prayers. This often produces three prayer sessions containing five separate prayers. Sunni schools generally place more restrictive conditions on combining prayers, with differences among the schools. Another visible feature is the small clay tablet, or *turbah*, often used by Twelver worshippers beneath the forehead during prostration. It provides an appropriate surface under Ja‘fari rules concerning prostration; the worship itself is directed to God. Shi‘a explanations of [combining prayers](https://al-islam.org/articles/laws-practices-why-do-shiah-combine-prayers) and [using a turbah](https://al-islam.org/articles/laws-practices-why-do-shiah-prostrate-turbah) clarify these practices.

The remembrance of Husayn, Ali’s son and Muhammad’s grandson, is especially important in Shi‘a religious life. In 680 CE, Husayn and his small group of supporters were killed at Karbala by forces serving the Umayyad ruler Yazid. His death became a powerful expression of unjust suffering and steadfast resistance to oppression. For many Shi‘a Muslims, remembering Karbala joins personal devotion to ethical reflection: believers consider what courage, loyalty, sacrifice, and responsibility require of them. The event’s importance extends beyond a dispute about government to a broader understanding of moral conduct. [Encyclopaedia Iranica’s account of Shi‘ism in Iraq](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iraq-x-shiites-of-iraq/) identifies Karbala as a crucial event in the tradition’s development.

Ashura, the tenth day of Muharram, commemorates Husayn’s death and is a major occasion of Shi‘a mourning. Observances can include sermons, poetry, processions, charitable meals, and visits to shrines. Their forms vary considerably across communities. Sunnis also honor Husayn, but the cycle of mourning associated with Karbala generally occupies a different place in Sunni religious life. Many Sunnis observe Ashura through voluntary fasting, drawing on prophetic traditions connecting the day with Moses and the deliverance of his people. These different emphases show how a shared religious calendar can carry distinct devotional meanings. They appear in [Pew’s discussion of Ashura](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2013/11/14/muslim-holiday-of-ashura-brings-into-focus-shia-sunni-differences/) and in the Sunni hadith collection [Sahih Muslim](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1130c).

The diversity within Shi‘ism places limits on comparisons that treat all Shi‘a Muslims as Twelvers. Ismaili Muslims recognize a different succession of Imams; Nizari Ismailis maintain a continuing line of living Imams known in modern times by the title Aga Khan. Zaydi Shi‘ism has its own understanding of leadership, historically emphasizing the qualifications and public action of an Imam descended from the Prophet’s family. Zaydis do not share the Twelver doctrine of the concealed twelfth Imam. These differences affect theology, institutions, and devotional practice. The St Andrews Encyclopaedia of Theology provides separate accounts of [Ismaili Shi‘ism](https://www.saet.ac.uk/Islam/IsmailiShiism) and [Zaydi Shi‘ism](https://www.saet.ac.uk/Islam/ZaydiShiism), demonstrating why the broader Shi‘a category requires careful qualification.

Sunni diversity likewise extends beyond the four legal schools. Sunni communities differ in theological interpretation, spiritual practice, local customs, and attitudes toward religious reform. Their members also hold varied political views. The same is true of Shi‘a communities, whose religious commitments do not determine a single position on government, citizenship, or public policy. These variations matter when interpreting sectarian conflict. Religious differences can supply powerful symbols and narratives, while struggles over political power, discrimination, resources, and security influence how those differences become mobilized. The [Council on Foreign Relations’ overview](https://www.cfr.org/articles/sunni-shia-divide-2) discusses both political rivalry and the long history of Sunni and Shi‘a Muslims living, worshipping, and forming families together.

An adequate comparison therefore considers several dimensions at once. Sunni and Shi‘a Muslims differ over the succession to Muhammad, the authority of the Imams, the transmission of religious knowledge, some legal rules, and the remembrance of sacred history. Those distinctions have lasting meaning for believers and deserve accurate explanation. At the same time, shared faith, ordinary social relationships, and internal diversity shape how religious identity is lived. A person’s Sunni or Shi‘a affiliation offers insight into a religious inheritance, but understanding that person also requires attention to their particular community, convictions, experiences, and choices.

Section 1

The first thing Daniel loved about Clara was her laugh. It reached him through an open window above the watchmaker’s shop. He looked up and saw a woman shaking rainwater from a broken umbrella. Behind her rose two narrow turrets with crooked copper roofs. Nobody else on Bell Street had turrets. Nobody else seemed quite so pleased by a ruined umbrella.

Clara lived in the old gatehouse beside the river. She repaired musical instruments in the rooms below its towers. She also had Tourette syndrome, which she mentioned when Daniel first brought her his grandfather’s violin. Sometimes her shoulder jerked, or a small sound interrupted her speech. Daniel asked whether she needed him to move the violin. She told him she needed him to stop holding it like a frightened chicken.

He laughed and loosened his grip. Clara examined the instrument beneath a yellow lamp. A strand of dark hair kept falling across her eyes. She pushed it back with the blunt end of a pencil. Daniel suddenly wished his grandfather had left him an entire orchestra. One damaged violin seemed an inadequate reason to return.

Fortunately, its repairs took three weeks. Daniel visited every Thursday with increasingly unconvincing questions. Clara answered each one while hiding a smile. Eventually she asked whether he wanted tea or another explanation of hide glue. He chose tea. They drank it in the eastern turret while rain rattled against the glass.

From that room, the river looked like a ribbon being slowly unrolled. Clara told him she had bought the gatehouse with her mother’s inheritance. Everyone had advised her to choose somewhere sensible. Instead, she had chosen a leaking roof and a view of migrating swallows. Daniel understood the decision immediately. By the time the violin was ready, he was in love.

Section 2

He did not tell her when he collected it. Instead, he asked whether she would join him for supper. Clara considered him over the rim of her teacup. Then she said she would, provided he stopped inventing problems with perfectly healthy instruments. Daniel promised to develop more honest conversational habits. She agreed to meet him on Saturday.

Their first supper lasted until the restaurant stacked chairs around them. Clara described a cello that had arrived with a mouse inside it. Daniel confessed that he sometimes talked to stubborn clocks. She admitted that she named particularly disagreeable customers after vegetables. He asked what vegetable he had been. Apparently, he had narrowly escaped becoming a turnip.

Over the following months, they learned each other’s ordinary habits. Clara forgot meals when a repair interested her. Daniel always saved the crispiest potatoes until last. She liked company after some difficult days and solitude after others. He learned to ask which kind of evening she wanted. Neither of them was especially good at admitting when they were tired.

Then an invitation arrived for the town’s midsummer exhibition. Clara had been asked to demonstrate the restoration of an antique harp. She practiced her talk in the western turret with Daniel sitting among dusty boxes. During the exhibition, a sharp vocal tic interrupted her explanation. A man near the front snickered into his hand. Daniel stepped forward and began explaining Clara’s condition to the room.

Clara stopped him before he finished. She completed her demonstration, answered questions, and packed her tools without looking at him. Outside, Daniel said he had only wanted to help. Clara told him she had been handling the room herself. What hurt was hearing him take over without asking. Daniel carried the harp case home beside her, painfully aware of how little an apology explained.

Section 3

The next evening, Daniel knocked on the gatehouse door. He had brought neither flowers nor a speech about his intentions. He apologized for speaking over her. Then he asked what she would have preferred him to do. Clara leaned against the doorframe and thought for a moment. She said he could have waited for her cue and helped with the harp afterward.

They talked until the workshop grew dark. Clara told him about the exhausting business of managing other people’s reactions. Daniel listened without searching for a sentence that would make everything better. Eventually she put the kettle on. He took that as an invitation to stay. This time, he checked.

A week later, a surveyor arrived to inspect the gatehouse. He found rotten supports beneath the western turret. The repairs would cost more than Clara had saved. Without them, that part of the house would have to be closed. Clara read the estimate twice at her kitchen table. Daniel sat beside her while she worked through the figures.

He asked whether she wanted help finding another builder. She did, and she also wanted someone to say the estimate was outrageous. Daniel supplied both services with enthusiasm. They obtained three quotations and discovered a small grant for historic buildings. Clara wrote the application while Daniel photographed the damaged beams. When the grant covered only half the work, she decided to sell several restored instruments.

They held the sale in the gatehouse courtyard on a bright September afternoon. A local quartet offered to play Clara’s instruments for prospective buyers. Daniel managed the receipts and kept the musicians supplied with tea. Clara moved between customers, explaining repairs and negotiating prices with unmistakable pleasure. By sunset, they had raised enough to begin the work. After everyone left, she kissed Daniel beneath the scaffolding.

Section 4

The repairs continued through a wet and inconvenient autumn. Dust settled inside cupboards that nobody remembered opening. Clara complained about the builders’ radio and then learned every song it played. Daniel spent weekends helping her move furniture away from falling plaster. They argued once about where to put an enormous cabinet. Clara won because Daniel had badly underestimated the width of the stairs.

When the western turret finally reopened, they carried supper upstairs on a tray. The new window fitted properly for the first time in decades. Clara stood beside it and watched lights appear along the river. Daniel put down the plates before he could lose his nerve. He told her he loved her. She turned around so quickly that he almost stepped into the soup.

Clara said she loved him too. She had been waiting to hear whether he might eventually mention it. Daniel admitted that he had rehearsed the conversation several times. In every rehearsal, he had sounded considerably more composed. Clara took his hand and asked whether the soup had survived. They ate it sitting on the floor because the chairs were still downstairs.

Daniel began staying at the gatehouse more often. Eventually, Clara cleared a cupboard for his clothes and complained when he failed to use it. His clocks occupied one end of the workshop. Her instruments occupied most of the rest. Her tics remained part of their days, sometimes troublesome and sometimes barely noticed. They kept asking each other what would help, and occasionally got the answer wrong.

The following spring, swallows returned to nest beneath the eastern roof. Clara watched them from the window where Daniel had first seen her. Downstairs, he was trying to repair the umbrella she still refused to throw away. She called for him to bring it up when he was finished. He arrived carrying it open, caught its edge in the doorway, and heard her laugh. There was room in the turret for both of them, once he folded the umbrella.

first names are among the earliest gifts we receive, yet their meanings develop throughout our lives. parents may choose them to honor relatives, preserve cultural traditions, express religious beliefs, or simply celebrate a pleasing sound. a name can therefore carry a family’s history before its bearer has a history of their own. although naming is often treated as a private decision, it also reflects wider patterns of migration, fashion, language, and belonging.

jasper illustrates how a first name can connect personal identity with associations that extend beyond any individual. it may bring to mind a gemstone, a fictional character, or someone remembered with affection. these associations influence first impressions, but they cannot fully describe the person who carries the name. over time, personality and experience reshape its meaning. what initially sounds unfamiliar can become comforting through friendship, while an ordinary name can become unforgettable through love.

first names also reveal a tension between individuality and community. an unusual name may offer distinction while requiring frequent explanation; a familiar name may create immediate recognition while offering less separation from others. neither choice determines a person’s future, though both can shape everyday encounters. respecting someone’s chosen name and learning its pronunciation acknowledge their right to define themselves. ultimately, a first name matters because people fill it with experience, turning an inherited word into a living expression of identity.

    Once lent out his books to a hen.
    It pecked at each page
    With scholarly rage,
    Then asked for the same books again.

    Packed sandwiches neatly in jars.

    He opened a store,
    Then caught twenty more,

    And laughter soon brought the house down.

    Once painted a door in midair.
    He knocked on it twice
    And found it quite nice
    When a breeze said, “Come in, take a chair!”

    Kept one little bird in his vest.
    It sorted his mail
    With a flick of its tail,
    Then slept on the stamps for a rest.

    His neighbor suggested a mute.
    He played for a bear

    He ran down the track

    They learned how to write

    That whistled a tune every week.

    Had a cow that could open his door.
    It wandered inside

    He forgot every line,

    Built a clock that would run on a bark.
    When a dog asked the time,
    It let out such a chime

    Went skating while stirring a stew.

Japan’s history stretches back tens of thousands of years. The *Jōmon* period featured hunter-gatherer communities and distinctive pottery. During the *Yayoi* period, wet-rice farming and metalworking spread from the Asian mainland, encouraging larger settlements and social hierarchies.

By the early centuries CE, the *Yamato* court was consolidating power. Influences from China and Korea—including Buddhism, writing, and government institutions—helped shape the emerging state. The Nara and *Heian* periods saw flourishing court culture, literature, and art, while the emperor’s political authority increasingly passed to powerful aristocratic families.

From the late twelfth century, military rulers called *shoguns* generally governed Japan, supported by *samurai* warriors. The Kamakura and Muromachi governments faced internal struggles, Mongol invasion attempts, and eventually prolonged civil warfare. In the late sixteenth century, successive warlords reunified the country.

The *Tokugawa* shogunate, established in 1603, brought more than 250 years of relative peace. It maintained a strict social order and tightly controlled foreign relations, while cities, commerce, and popular culture expanded. Western pressure, particularly American naval visits beginning in 1853, helped destabilize its rule.

The *Meiji Restoration* of 1868 restored imperial government and launched rapid industrialization, military reform, and institutional change. Japan became an imperial power, acquiring Taiwan, annexing Korea, and expanding into China. Its wars of conquest culminated in *World War II*, which ended with Japan’s surrender in 1945 after devastating warfare, atomic bombings, and Soviet entry into the war against Japan.

Under the Allied occupation, Japan adopted a democratic constitution, retained the emperor as a symbolic figure, and renounced war. Postwar reconstruction produced extraordinary economic growth. By the late twentieth century, Japan was a leading industrial economy, though the collapse of its asset bubble in the early 1990s began a prolonged period of economic difficulty.

Write a pitch deck for a startup that aims to make a new social network that focuses on the board game society.

---

**1. BoardCircle**
*Find your people. Fill your table.*

A social network that helps board game players discover compatible groups, organize sessions, and build lasting friendships through play.

**2. The problem**
Owning a great game is easy. Getting the right people around the table is harder.

Players juggle group chats, event listings, and spreadsheets to coordinate sessions. Newcomers struggle to find welcoming groups. Organizers repeatedly chase RSVPs and explain what each session involves.

**3. The solution**
BoardCircle connects discovery, planning, and community in one place.

Players find nearby sessions based on game preferences, experience, availability, and accessibility needs. Hosts organize events with clear expectations, reliable RSVPs, and automatic waitlists.

**4. The product**
The core experience follows a simple journey:

- Create a profile with favorite games, interests, and availability.
- Discover compatible players, clubs, and upcoming sessions.
- Join a table or host your own.
- Stay connected through recurring groups and shared game collections.

Privacy controls, reporting tools, and optional public meeting locations support comfortable participation.

**5. Our first customers**
We start with people who already bring others together: recurring hosts, board game cafés, and local clubs.

These organizers supply consistent events that attract players. Our initial player audience is enthusiasts seeking regular sessions and newcomers looking for an approachable first table.

**6. Why BoardCircle wins**
General social platforms help people talk. BoardCircle helps them play together.

Our advantage is structured information: player count, session length, teaching availability, complexity preferences, and attendance history. Every completed session improves future recommendations.

The central measure of success is repeat play with people users meet through BoardCircle.

**7. Business model**
Core profiles, discovery, and event participation are free.

Proposed pricing to test:

- **Player Plus — $5/month:** advanced collection tools, saved searches, and personalized alerts.
- **Organizer — $49/month:** recurring event management, membership administration, and attendance insights.
- **Ticketed events:** an optional service fee on paid bookings.

**8. Go to market**
Launch in one city and build a dependable calendar of sessions before expanding.

Recruit founding cafés and clubs, help experienced hosts establish recurring tables, and run beginner-friendly events. Invite links turn each organized session into a path for new members to join.

Expand when the first community demonstrates repeat attendance and sustained organizer activity.

**9. Market opportunity**
Our initial market is local communities that already meet regularly to play.

Expansion follows three paths: more cities, more organizer subscriptions, and additional services for conventions and publishers.

Market sizing will use verified counts of reachable players, active venues, and achievable subscription conversion.

**10. Validation and milestones**
This is a proposed startup; the following are targets, not existing traction.

Within 12 months:

- Secure 10 venue partners.
- Activate 50 recurring hosts.
- Reach 100 completed sessions per month.
- Demonstrate repeat attendance and willingness to pay.

The first experiments will test whether better matching and easier coordination produce more recurring groups.

**11. Team and investment**
The founding team needs strengths in consumer product development, community operations, and partnerships with gaming venues.

We are seeking an illustrative **$750,000 pre-seed investment** for 18 months: 60% product and engineering, 25% community development, and 15% operations.
